noun:Haus.tx: From Middle High German hūs, from Old High German hūs, from Proto-West Germanic *hūs, from Proto-Germanic *hūsą. Cognate with Old Frisian hūs, Low German Hus, Huus, Dutch huis, Icelandic hús, Faroese hús, Danish hus, Norwegian hus, Swedish hus, English house. Doublet of House.

adj:hell.tx: From Middle High German hel (“resounding, loud, shining, bright”), from Old High German hel (“resounding”), from Proto-Germanic *halliz (“resounding”), from Proto-Germanic *hellaną (“to resound, make a sound”), from Proto-Indo-European *kelh₁- (“to call, make noise”). Cognate with Dutch hel.

adv:her.tx: From Middle High German hër, hëre, from Old High German hëra, which corresponds to hier in the same way as dara (“thither”) to dār (“there”). Cognate to Dutch her, Low German her, and possibly Gothic 𐌷𐌹𐍂𐌹 (hiri).

intj:hi.tx: Borrowed from English hi, from 1990s digitalization.

adv:hier.tx: From Middle High German hier, from Old High German hier, from Proto-West Germanic *hēr. Cognate with Dutch hier, English here, Swedish här. The predominant form in Middle High German and throughout modern dialects of High German is hie (and variants) with loss of the final -r. The form hier began to gain ground from the late 16th century (in spite of Luther’s usage), which may point to influence …

intj:hier.tx: From Middle High German hier, from Old High German hier, from Proto-West Germanic *hēr. Cognate with Dutch hier, English here, Swedish här. The predominant form in Middle High German and throughout modern dialects of High German is hie (and variants) with loss of the final -r. The form hier began to gain ground from the late 16th century (in spite of Luther’s usage), which may point to influence …

adj:hold.tx: From Middle High German holt, from Old High German hold, from Proto-West Germanic *holþ, from Proto-Germanic *hulþaz. Cognates include Gothic 𐌷𐌿𐌻𐌸𐍃 (hulþs, “clement”) and Old Norse hollr ( > Danish huld).

adj:high.tx: Borrowed from English high. Doublet of hoch.

adj:hart.tx: From Middle High German hart, Old High German hart, from Proto-West Germanic *hard(ī), from Proto-Germanic *harduz, from Proto-Indo-European *kortús (“strong; powerful”). Cognate with Low German hard, hart, Dutch hard, English hard, Danish hård.

adv:hart.tx: From Middle High German hart, Old High German hart, from Proto-West Germanic *hard(ī), from Proto-Germanic *harduz, from Proto-Indo-European *kortús (“strong; powerful”). Cognate with Low German hard, hart, Dutch hard, English hard, Danish hård.

noun:Herz.tx: PIE word *ḱḗr Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *ḱerd- Proto-Indo-European *ḱérd Proto-Germanic *hertô Proto-West Germanic *hertā Old High German hërza Middle High German hërze German Herz From Middle High German hërze, from Old High German hërza, from Proto-West Germanic *hertā, from Proto-Germanic *hertô (“heart”), from Proto-Indo-European *ḱḗr (“heart”). Cognate with Dutch hart, English …

noun:Honig.tx: From Middle High German honic, honec, hönic, hünic, from Old High German honag, from Proto-West Germanic *hunag, from Proto-Germanic *hunagą. Cognate with English honey.

intj:hallo.tx: Originally used as a call to the ferryman on the other side of the bank; related to Old High German holā, emphatic imperative of holōn (“to fetch, used especially in hailing a ferryman”), from Proto-West Germanic *holōn (“to fetch”). Also see French holà (“hey! stop!”).

noun:Hesse.tx: From Middle High German Hesse, from Old High German Hesso, possibly ultimately derived from Proto-Germanic *hatjaną (“to persecute; hate”). Compare Chatti, Chasuarii, Chattuarii.

noun:Heimweh.tx: Heim + Weh. Originally a medical term in Switzerland. Cognate to Alemannic German Häiwee, Bavarian Haimweh (Upper Austrian), Low German Heimweih.

noun:Herbst.tx: From Middle High German herbest, from Old High German herbist, from Proto-West Germanic *harbist. Compare Dutch herfst, Low German Harvst, West Frisian hjerst, English harvest.

adj:herb.tx: From Middle High German hare, here (inflected harwe, herwe), from Old High German *haro, from Proto-West Germanic *haru.

adj:heilig.tx: From Middle High German heilic (hailig, heilec), from Old High German heilag, from Proto-West Germanic *hailag. Compare Low German hillig, Dutch heilig, English holy, Danish hellig, Swedish helig.

intj:hüa.tx: Onomatopoeic. Compare Dutch ju, French hue.

noun:Helikopter.tx: Borrowed from English helicopter, from French hélicoptère, from Ancient Greek ἕλιξ (hélix, “spiral”) + πτερόν (pterón, “wing”).

noun:Heuschrecke.tx: From Middle High German höuschrecke, from Old High German houwiscrecko. Analysable as Heu (“hay”) + schrecken (“to jump up”). Originally a masculine that developed into a feminine under the influence of the frequently used plural (a common development in modern German); compare the southern alternative form.

noun:Herr.tx: From Middle High German hērre, hërre, from Old High German hēriro, hērro, originally comparative of hēr (“grey-haired, noble, venerable”, whence German hehr), a semantic loan from Latin senior (“elder”). Ultimately from Proto-Germanic *hairaz (“grey”). Cognate with Dutch heer, Old English hār, English hoar, Old Norse hárr; compare also modern German hehr (“noble, holy”), herrschen (“to rule”).

verb:husten.tx: From Middle High German huosten, from Old High German huostōn from Proto-Germanic *hwōstōną. Cognate with Dutch hoesten, English whoost, Swedish hosta.

intj:halt.tx: From the verb halten (“to hold; to stop”).

adv:halt.tx: From Middle High German halt, pertaining to Old High German halto (“soon, fast”). Ultimately from Proto-Germanic *haldiz (related to *halþaz (“inclined”)), an adverbial comparative like *batiz.

verb:helfen.tx: From Middle High German hëlfen, from Old High German hëlfan, from Proto-West Germanic *helpan, from Proto-Germanic *helpaną, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱelb-, *ḱelp-. Cognate with Low German helpen, Dutch helpen, English help, Danish hjælpe, Norwegian Bokmål hjelpe.

As to the variation between ⟨nd⟩ and ⟨nt⟩: In Upper German texts, West Germanic *nd regularly surfaces as Old High German ⟨nt⟩, but Middle High German ⟨nd⟩ (alongside rare ⟨nt⟩ spellings). As to the variation between ⟨nd⟩ and ⟨nt⟩: In Upper German texts, West Germanic *nd regularly surfaces as Old High German ⟨nt⟩, but Middle High German ⟨nd⟩ (alongside rare ⟨nt⟩ spellings). adv:hinaus.tx: From Middle High German hinūz, from Old High German hinaūz. By surface analysis, hin + aus.

adv:heraus.tx: From Middle High German herūz, herūʒ, harūz, from Old High German heraūz (“out of here; forth”), equivalent to her- (“to or over here; hither”, prefix implying movement) + aus (“out”). Compare hinaus (“out from here”) and daraus (“out from there”) and archaic English hereout (“out of here”).

verb:heißen.tx: From Middle High German heiȥen, from Old High German heiȥan, from Proto-West Germanic *haitan, from Proto-Germanic *haitaną. Cognates Cognate with Bavarian haßn, hoaßn, Yiddish הייסן (heysn), Dutch heten, Low German heten, heiten, hight (“to name; to be named”), Old Norse heita, Gothic 𐌷𐌰𐌹𐍄𐌰𐌽 (haitan). Compare also with English hest, behest.

noun:Horizont.tx: 16th century, borrowed from Latin horizōn, horizontis, from Ancient Greek ὁρίζων (horízōn), from ὅρος (hóros, “boundary”).

noun:Handschuh.tx: Inherited from Middle High German hantschuoch, from Old High German hantscuoh, from Proto-West Germanic *handuskōh. Equivalent to Hand (“hand”) + Schuh (“shoe”). Cognate with Bavarian Håndschuach, German Low German Handsch, Handschoh, Hansch, Luxembourgish Händsch, Dutch handschoen, Danish handske, Norwegian Bokmål hanske, Norwegian Nynorsk hanske, handske (obsolete), Swedish handske, Faroese …

noun:Haar.tx: From Middle High German and Old High German hār, from Proto-West Germanic *hār, from Proto-Germanic *hērą, from Proto-Indo-European *keres- (“rough hair, bristle”). Compare Dutch haar, West Frisian hier, English hair, Danish hår.

noun:Hag.tx: From Middle High German hac, from Old High German hag, from Proto-West Germanic *hagō. Cognate with Dutch haag, Swedish hage, Old English hæg. Doublet of Hain.

noun:Hai.tx: Early 17th century, from Dutch haai, from Middle Dutch haey (15th c.), from Old Norse hár, há- (“shark”).

noun:Hall.tx: From Middle High German hal, from hellen, from Old High German hellan (“to resound, ring out”), ultimately from the root of hell (“bright, clear”). Cognate with Middle Low German hal (“loud; echoing; clear”), Old High German hellan (“to sound; resound”), Old English hiellan (“to make a noise; sound; blast”).

noun:Halm.tx: From Middle High German halm, from Old High German halm, from Proto-West Germanic *halm, from Proto-Germanic *halmaz, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱolh₂mos.

noun:Hals.tx: From Middle High German hals, from Old High German hals, from Proto-West Germanic *hals, from Proto-Germanic *halsaz.

noun:Halt.tx: Inherited from Middle High German halt, equivalent to a deverbal from halten.

noun:Hammer.tx: From Middle High German hamer, from Old High German hamar, from Proto-West Germanic *hamar, from Proto-Germanic *hamaraz, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂eḱmoros, from *h₂éḱmō (“stone”). Compare Low German Hamer, Dutch hamer, English hammer, West Frisian hammer, Danish hammer, Swedish hammare.

noun:Hamster.tx: From Middle High German hamster, from Old High German hamastra, hamustro, probably from Old East Slavic хомѣсторъ (xoměstorŭ), хомѣстаръ (xoměstarŭ). Further explained as a borrowing into Slavic from Iranian, compare Avestan 𐬵𐬀𐬨𐬀𐬉𐬯𐬙𐬀𐬭- (hamaēstar-, “who throws down (in this case: corn stalks), oppresses”). Alternatively, a compound of (1) хомѣкъ (xoměkŭ, “hamster”), from Proto-Balto-Slavic …

noun:Hand.tx: From Middle High German hant, from Old High German hant, from Proto-West Germanic *handu, from Proto-Germanic *handuz. Compare Dutch hand, English hand, West Frisian hân, Danish hånd, Gothic 𐌷𐌰𐌽𐌳𐌿𐍃 (handus), Yiddish האַנט (hant).

noun:Handy.tx: Some sources claim the existence of an early English preform. Perhaps from English handie-talkie, apparently used as a Motorola product name based on walkie-talkie. Or perhaps derived from English handheld transceiver, coined by CB radio users, later informally applied to the first mobile phones, and soon found in product names. Others assert the use for a phone is exclusively German, possibly as …

noun:Happen.tx: Adopted in the 18th century from German Low German, which may have borrowed it from Dutch. A Dutch verb happen (“to snap”) is attested from the 16th century on; all ultimately imitative of children's speech (Kindersprache), akin to (South) Proto-Slavic *xapati. Compare also contemporary Dutch hap. It is unsettled whether there is any relation with Old French happer.

noun:Harem.tx: From Ottoman Turkish حرم (harem), from Arabic حَرَم (ḥaram).

noun:Hast.tx: 16th century, from Middle Low German hāst, from Middle Dutch haest, a borrowing from Old French haste, itself borrowed from Frankish *hai(f)st, from Proto-Germanic *haifstiz. See English haste for more.

noun:Haut.tx: From Middle High German hūt, from Old High German hūt, from Proto-West Germanic *hūdi, from Proto-Germanic *hūdiz, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)kewH-.

noun:Heck.tx: From Middle Low German heck (“wooden fencing”), from Old Saxon *hekki, from Proto-West Germanic *hakkju. The sense “back of a ship” because the position of the helmsman in the stern was enclosed by such a fence. Cognate to Dutch hek, English hatch.

noun:Heft.tx: 18th-century backformation from heften (“to fasten”), from *haftijaną (“to bind, secure”).

noun:Held.tx: From Middle High German helt (genitive heldes), from Old High German helid, from Proto-West Germanic *haliþ (“hero”). Cognate with Old English hæleþ (English health), Old Saxon helið (Dutch held), West Frisian held, Old Norse halr, hǫlðr (Norwegian Nynorsk hauld). Outside of Germanic, possibly also related to Ancient Greek κέλωρ (kélōr), Tocharian B kālyśke (“boy”).

noun:Helium.tx: Borrowed from New Latin hēlium, from Ancient Greek ἥλιος (hḗlios, “sun”). The name of the gas was a derivation from the Ancient Greek term for Sun because helium was the first element to be found in the Sun's atmosphere via spectroscopy.

noun:Helm.tx: From Middle High German hëlm, from Old High German hëlm, from Proto-West Germanic *helm, from Proto-Germanic *helmaz. Compare Low German Helm, Dutch helm, English helm, Danish hjelm.

noun:Herd.tx: From Middle High German hërt, from Old High German hërd, from Proto-West Germanic *herþ. Cognate with Dutch haard, English hearth.

noun:Heroin.tx: Invented as a brand name by the German pharmaceutical company Bayer, which started marketing heroine in 1895. The name was coined to evoke heroisch (“heroic”), ultimately from Greek ἥρως (hḗrōs, “hero”).

noun:Himmel.tx: From Middle High German himel, from Old High German himil, from Proto-West Germanic *himil.

noun:Hockey.tx: Borrowed from English hockey. The archaic pronunciation in /-aɪ̯/ is a spelling pronunciation; the now usual form in /-e/ is also influenced by the spelling.

noun:Holocaust.tx: Unadapted borrowing from English Holocaust. Popularized through the American TV production Holocaust (1978, first broadcast in Germany in January 1979), it was selected word of the year in Germany in December 1979.

noun:Horde.tx: From Late Middle High German horde (15th c.), from Old Polish orda, from Old East Slavic [script needed] (orda), itself from Classical Mongolian ᠣᠷᠳ᠋ᠤ (ordu) or from a Kipchak language, ultimately from Proto-Turkic *ordu (“camp”).

noun:Horn.tx: From Middle High German horn, from Old High German horn, from Proto-West Germanic *horn, from Proto-Germanic *hurną, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *ḱer-. Compare Low German Horn, Hoorn, Hurn; Höärn (Altmärkisch); Häörn (Haön) (Münsterländisch), Dutch hoorn, English horn, Danish horn and Swedish horn.

noun:Horror.tx: Borrowed from Latin horror; cf. also English horror.

noun:Hose.tx: From Middle High German hose, from Old High German hosa, from Proto-West Germanic *hosā.

noun:Hostie.tx: From Middle High German hostie, ostie, from Latin hostia.

noun:House.tx: Borrowed from English house. Doublet of Haus.

noun:Hulk.tx: From Middle High German holche, from Old High German holcho.

noun:Hummer.tx: 16th century, from Middle Low German *hummer, itself from Old Norse humarr, perhaps through early Norwegian (as many lobsters were caught off the coast of Norway). From the same North Germanic source Modern Low German Hummer, Plautdietsch Humma, Dutch hommer.

noun:Humor.tx: Borrowed from Latin hūmor; later a semantic loan from English humour.

noun:Hund.tx: Inherited from Middle High German hunt, from Old High German hunt, from Proto-West Germanic *hund, from Proto-Germanic *hundaz, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱwṓ. Cognates Cognates include Dutch hond, English hound, Danish hund, Icelandic hundur, and Gothic 𐌷𐌿𐌽𐌳𐍃 (hunds).

noun:Hunger.tx: From Middle High German hunger, from Old High German hungar, from Proto-West Germanic *hungr, from Proto-Germanic *hungruz.

noun:Hunt.tx: Originated as a metaphorical application of Hund (“dog”) to small minecarts (16th c.), with final lenition generalized across all forms, though unlenited forms also still exist.

noun:Husten.tx: From Middle High German huoste, from Old High German huosto, from Proto-West Germanic *hwōstō, from Proto-Germanic *hwōstô.

noun:Hut.tx: From Middle High German huot, from Old High German huot, from Proto-West Germanic *hōd, from Proto-Germanic *hōdaz, possibly from a Proto-Indo-European *kadʰ- (“to protect”), but the existence of such a root is doubtful. Cognate to Dutch hoed, English hood.

noun:Hymne.tx: Borrowed from Latin hymnus, from Ancient Greek ὕμνος (húmnos).

verb:haben.tx: From Middle High German haben, from Old High German habēn (akin to Old Saxon hebbian, Old Norse hafa (Swedish hava/ha), Old Frisian habba, Gothic 𐌷𐌰𐌱𐌰𐌽 (haban), Old English habban), from Proto-West Germanic *habbjan, from Proto-Germanic *habjaną, from Proto-Indo-European *kap- (“to grasp”). Cognates include Bavarian håbn, Yiddish האָבן (hobn), Dutch hebben, English have, Danish have.

noun:Habicht.tx: From Middle High German habech, from Old High German habuch, habuh, from Proto-West Germanic *habuk. Compare Dutch havik, Low German Haavk, English hawk, Swedish hök, Norwegian hauk.

noun:Hase.tx: From Middle High German has(e), from Old High German haso, from Proto-West Germanic *hasō, from Proto-Germanic *hesô, from an Indo-European root originally meaning grey.

noun:Hasenscharte.tx: From Middle High German hasinscharte. By surface analysis, Hase (“hare”) + -n- + Scharte (“notch”). So called because of the similarity to the outer form of a hare’s lip. Compare already Old English hærsceard.

noun:Hauer.tx: From hauen + -er. Compare Dutch houwer, English hewer.

verb:hauen.tx: From Middle High German houwen, Old High German houwan, from Proto-West Germanic *hauwan, from Proto-Germanic *hawwaną. Cognate with English hew.

noun:Hacke.tx: 15th century, from Middle Low German hakke, from Proto-Germanic *hak(k)-, perhaps related to *hakô. Cognate with Dutch hak. The word also existed in Old High German as hakka (“animal heel”), but this had no attested continuation in Middle High German.

verb:hacken.tx: From Middle High German hacken, from Old High German hacchōn, from Proto-West Germanic *hakkōn, from Proto-Germanic *hakkōną (“to hack, chop; to hoe”). Cognate with Dutch hakken, English hack.

noun:Hackfresse.tx: Probably from Hack(fleisch) (“minced meat”) + Fresse (“mouth, mug”, derogatory).

noun:Harn.tx: From Middle High German and Old High German harn, from the Proto-Indo-European root *(s)ḱer- (“dung, filth”). Cognate with Lithuanian šarmas (“lye”) (for semantic connection, compare lant). Exclusively High German form without s-mobile alongside Proto-Germanic *skarną (“dung”), whence dialectal English sharn and German Schierling (“hemlock”).

noun:Hof.tx: From Middle High German hof, from Old High German hof, from Proto-West Germanic *hof, from Proto-Germanic *hufą (“hill, farm”). See there for cognates.

noun:Halle.tx: From Middle High German halle, from Old High German halla, from Proto-West Germanic *hallu. Compare Low German Hall, Dutch hal, English hall, Danish hall, Swedish hall.

noun:Hiobsbotschaft.tx: From Hiob + -s- + Botschaft. From the Biblical story in which many bad things happen to Hiob (“Job”).

noun:Herberge.tx: From Middle High German herbërge, from Old High German heribërga, from Proto-West Germanic *harjabergu.

noun:Heer.tx: From Middle High German her, from Old High German heri, from Proto-West Germanic *hari, from Proto-Germanic *harjaz, from Proto-Indo-European *ker- (“war, struggle”). Cognates include Old Norse herr (“crowd, troops”, > Danish hær (“troops”)), Dutch heer (“army”), Gothic 𐌷𐌰𐍂𐌾𐌹𐍃 (harjis, “army, host”), Old English here (“army”). Relation to Sanskrit कुल (kula, “flock, herd, family”) has been …

noun:Handel.tx: From handeln, later specialized to its current meaning.

verb:handeln.tx: From Middle High German handeln, from Old High German hantalōn, from Proto-West Germanic *handulōn. By surface analysis, Hand + -eln.

noun:Handlung.tx: From Middle High German handelunge, from Old High German hantalunga. By surface analysis, handeln + -ung.

noun:Hütte.tx: From Middle High German hütte, from Old High German hutta (“hut, cottage”), possibly from Proto-Germanic *hudjǭ, though the word is originally exclusively High German. Further origin unknown. Some theories link it to Proto-Indo-European *(s)kewt- (“to deck; cover; covering; skin”). All related words in European languages are borrowings from Old High German. Compare Dutch hut, French hutte, English hut, etc.

noun:Herde.tx: From Middle High German hërt, from Old High German hërta, from Proto-West Germanic *herdu. The modern consonantism is Central and Low German (compare Middle Low German hērde). Cognate with English herd, Danish hjord, Swedish hjord, Gothic 𐌷𐌰𐌹𐍂𐌳𐌰 (hairda).

noun:Hebamme.tx: From Middle High German hebamme (15th century), heveamme (13 ct.), from Old High German hevanna (“midwife”), later altered to Hebamme to resemble Amme (“wet nurse”) (amme). This development is still reflected in modern German, inasmuch as the word can either be pronounced as a compound ("Heb-Amme") or as one word ("Hebamme").

verb:heben.tx: From Middle High German heben, heven (rarer heffen), from Old High German heffen, heven, from Proto-West Germanic *habbjan. Compare Dutch heffen, English heave, Danish hæve. Doublet of hieven and kapieren. The -b- is regular in the past tense and participle. In Middle High German the paradigm was regularised by spreading -b- to the present tense; reinforced in East Central German by the local …

noun:Hügel.tx: From Middle High German hogil, diminutive of houc, from Old High German houg.

noun:Heimchen.tx: Heim + -chen. In the figurative sense popularized by the German title of Charles Dickens' The Cricket on the Hearth (1845), Das Heimchen am Herde.

noun:Heim.tx: From Middle High German heim, from Old High German heim, from Proto-West Germanic *haim. Cognate with Dutch heem, English home, Danish hjem.

adv:heim.tx: From Heim (“home”). Compare Middle High German heime (“home, at home”, adverb), from Old High German heime, heimi (“home, at home”, adverb).

noun:Heimat.tx: First attested in the 11th century. From Middle High German heimuote, heimüete, from Old High German heimōti, heimuoti, from Proto-West Germanic *haimōdī (“homeland”). Compare Bavarian Hoamat, Silesian East Central German Heemte.

noun:Hasse.tx: From the Viennese dialect word hass (“hot”); thus literally, “a hot one”.

noun:Hahn.tx: From Middle High German hane, from Old High German hano, from Proto-West Germanic *hanō, from Proto-Germanic *hanô. Compare Dutch haan, Danish hane.

adv:hin.tx: From Middle High German hin, from Old High German hina. Cognate with Dutch heen. Compare also English hence.

adj:hin.tx: From Middle High German hin, from Old High German hina. Cognate with Dutch heen. Compare also English hence.

noun:Holz.tx: From Middle High German holz, from Old High German holz, from Proto-West Germanic *holt, from Proto-Germanic *hultą. Compare English holt (“thicket, copse; an otter's den”).

noun:Höhe.tx: From Middle High German hœhe, from Old High German hōhī. Analysable as hoch + -e.

adj:hoch.tx: From Middle High German hōch, from Old High German hōh, from Proto-West Germanic *hauh, from Proto-Germanic *hauhaz, from Proto-Indo-European *kewk-, a suffixed form of *kew-. Compare Dutch hoog, Low German hoog, English high, Swedish hög. The irregular declension from the stem hoh- is due to the development of Old High German -h-, which in Middle High German became /x/ in coda position, but /h/ …

adv:hoch.tx: From Middle High German hōch, from Old High German hōh, from Proto-West Germanic *hauh, from Proto-Germanic *hauhaz, from Proto-Indo-European *kewk-, a suffixed form of *kew-. Compare Dutch hoog, Low German hoog, English high, Swedish hög. The irregular declension from the stem hoh- is due to the development of Old High German -h-, which in Middle High German became /x/ in coda position, but /h/ …

noun:Hochzeit.tx: From Middle High German hōchzīt, hōchgezīt, from (only plural) hōhūn gizīti (“high celebration”), equivalent to hoch (“high”) + Zeit (“time”).

noun:Hochstapler.tx: Thieves' argot; from Stappler "beggar", not related to stapeln. Hochstapler means a beggar acting like he is originally high class, but in a dire situation.

noun:Hummel.tx: From Middle High German humbel, hummel, from Old High German humbal, humbala, humbalo. Cognate with Dutch hommel, Danish humlebi, Swedish humla. Eventually probably onomatopoeic and related with English hum. Compare English bumblebee, which has Middle English bombeln ("to buzz") as its first element.

noun:Haube.tx: From Middle High German hoube, hūbe, from Old High German hūba, from Proto-West Germanic *hūbā, from Proto-Germanic *hūbǭ.

noun:Himbeere.tx: By renewed adaptation to Beere from earlier and still dialectal Himper, by assimilation (as in Wimper) from Middle High German hintber, from Old High German hintberi, from Proto-West Germanic *hindibaʀi. Compare (dialectal) English hindberry, (dialectal) Dutch hennebes, hinnebes, Danish hindbær. Equivalent to Hinde (“hind, doe”) + Beere (“berry”).

noun:Heidelbeere.tx: From Heidel + Beere. The first part is a regional derivation from Heide for a sense of "that which grows in the heath" (akin to Eichel from Eiche) which has only become standard in this compound.

noun:Heide.tx: From Middle High German heide, from Old High German heida, from Proto-West Germanic *haiþi, from Proto-Germanic *haiþī. Cognate with English heath.

noun:Halbkugel.tx: halb (“half”) + Kugel (“sphere”), a calque of New Latin hemisphaerium, attested in scientific or technical literature from ca. the 1790s.

adj:halb.tx: From Middle High German halp, from Old High German halb, from Proto-West Germanic *halb, from Proto-Germanic *halbaz. Compare Dutch half, English half, Danish halv.

adv:halb.tx: From Middle High German halp, from Old High German halb, from Proto-West Germanic *halb, from Proto-Germanic *halbaz. Compare Dutch half, English half, Danish halv.

verb:halbieren.tx: Inherited from Middle High German halbieren. By surface analysis, halb + -ieren.

noun:Hirsch.tx: From Middle High German hirs, from older hirʐ(e), from Old High German hiruz, from Proto-West Germanic *herut, from Proto-Germanic *herutaz. Cognate with Dutch hert, English hart. When the Old High German -u- was lost by syncope (in inflected forms), the fricative /s̄/ came to stand after a consonant, which regularly it never did. This anomaly was then removed by replacing /s̄/ either with /s̠/ …

noun:Hälfte.tx: From Middle Low German helfte, derived from half (“half”). The form entered Early Modern German via Central German. Equivalent to halb (“half”) + -te. The alternation -b- ↔ -ft- has not been levelled, probably because the same alternation occurs also—for different reasons—in native High German words (compare schreiben ↔ Schrift). Cognate with Dutch helft.

num:hundert.tx: From Middle High German hundert, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *hundaradą, from *hundą (< Proto-Indo-European *ḱm̥tóm) + *radą (“count”). The Duden derives Middle High German hundert from Old Saxon hunderod.

noun:Hanf.tx: From Middle High German hanef, hanif, hanf, from Old High German hanaf, from Proto-West Germanic *hanapi, from Proto-Germanic *hanapiz. Compare Dutch hennep, English hemp, Danish hamp. Also cognate with Ancient Greek κάνναβις (kánnabis), whence the doublet Cannabis.

noun:Hänfling.tx: Hanf + -ling The bird was so called for its fondness for hemp seeds (cf. English linnet). The colloquial usage for a person is by comparison to a hemp plant (cf. English beanpole).

noun:Hafen.tx: From Middle Low German havene. The word was already borrowed into Middle High German habene; the modern form with -f- is a later adaptation once again based on the Middle Low German form. Ultimately from Proto-Germanic *habnō. Cognate to Dutch haven and English haven.

noun:Hirn.tx: From Middle High German hirne, hërne, from Old High German hirni (“brain”), from Proto-West Germanic *hirʀnī.

noun:Haifisch.tx: Explanatory compound from Hai (“shark”) + Fisch (“fish”). Compare with Yiddish הײַפֿיש (hayfish).

noun:Hagel.tx: From Middle High German hagel, from Old High German hagal, from Proto-Germanic *haglaz.

noun:Haufen.tx: From a merger of Middle High German hūfe (hūf), houf (houfe), from Old High German hūfo (more southern) and houf (more northern), from Proto-Germanic *hūpô and its ablaut variant *haupaz, respectively. With the former is cognate Middle Low German hūpe, with the latter Dutch hoop, English heap. Already in Middle High German the two forms began to influence each other such that the originally weak …

noun:Heu.tx: From Middle High German höuwe, höu, from Old High German hewi, houwi, hou, from Proto-West Germanic *hawi, from Proto-Germanic *hawją. Cognate with Old Norse hey (Danish hø), English hay, Gothic 𐌷𐌰𐍅𐌹 (hawi).

adj:homogen.tx: Borrowed from Ancient Greek ὁμογενής (homogenḗs, “of the same kind”), from ὁμός (homós, “same”) + γένος (génos, “kind”). Equivalent to homo- + -gen.

verb:hellen.tx: From Middle High German hëllen, from Old High German hëllan, from Proto-Germanic *hellaną (“to resound”).

noun:Herzog.tx: From Middle High German herzog, herzoge, from Old High German herizogo, and ultimately from Proto-West Germanic *harjatogō (“army leader”).

noun:Herzogin.tx: From Middle High German herzoginne, equivalent to Herzog + -in.

adj:hurtig.tx: Middle High German hurteclich, from hurt, from Old French hurt (French heurt).

verb:huren.tx: From Middle High German huoren, from Old High German huorōn, from Proto-Germanic *hōrōną.

noun:Hure.tx: From Middle High German huore, from Old High German huora, from Proto-Germanic *hōrǭ, from Proto-Indo-European *kéh₂ros (“dear, loved”). Cognate with Dutch hoer, English whore, Danish hore, Swedish hora.

verb:hören.tx: From Middle High German hœren, from Old High German hōren. Compare Dutch horen, English hear, Danish høre.

noun:Hölle.tx: From Middle High German helle, from Old High German hella, hellia, from Proto-West Germanic *hallju, from Proto-Germanic *haljō, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *ḱel- (“to cover, hide, conceal”). Compare Low German Hell, Dutch hel, English hell, Icelandic hel, helvíti.

adj:heil.tx: From Middle High German heil, from Old High German heil, from Proto-West Germanic *hail, from Proto-Germanic *hailaz, from Proto-Indo-European *kéh₂ilos (“healthy, whole”). In older High German only used of the human body and soul; the modern use also of things is based on Middle Low German hêl, from Old Saxon hēl. The more general sense “whole, entire” did not establish itself in standard German …

verb:halten.tx: From Middle High German halten, from Old High German haltan, from Proto-West Germanic *haldan, from Proto-Germanic *haldaną. Cognate with Bavarian hoidn, Low German holden, Dutch houden, holen, English hold, Danish holde, Icelandic halda, Swedish hålla.

adj:heiß.tx: From Middle High German and Old High German heiz, from Proto-West Germanic *hait. Akin to Old Saxon het, Dutch heet, English hot, Danish hed (“hot”).

verb:hassen.tx: From Middle High German haȥȥen, from Old High German haȥȥōn, from Proto-Germanic *hatāną.

noun:Hitze.tx: From Middle High German hitze, from Old High German hizza, from Proto-West Germanic *hittjā, from Proto-Germanic *hitjǭ (“heat”). Cognate with Dutch hitte. Also related with English heat.

verb:hoffen.tx: From Middle High German hoffen (12th c.), from northern Old High German *hoffōn, from Proto-West Germanic *hopōn. It is uncertain whether the (unattested but probable) Old High German form was inherited or rather borrowed from Old Dutch hopon with implementation of the High German consonantism (which was then still entirely predictable). In fact, some scholars consider that all continental forms …

noun:Harfe.tx: From Middle High German harpfe, from Old High German harfa, from Proto-West Germanic *harpā, from Proto-Germanic *harpǭ. Akin to Bavarian Harpfn, Old Saxon harpa, Dutch harp, English harp, Danish harpe. Doublet of Harpfe.

noun:Haupt.tx: From Middle High German houbet, höubet, from Old High German houbit, from Proto-West Germanic *haubid, from Proto-Germanic *haubudą, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *káput. The standardized form without umlaut is from Upper German, in which -ou- did not undergo umlaut before labials. The Central German form with umlaut is preserved in Häuptling and zu Häupten. Cognate with Dutch hoofd, German …

noun:Hopfen.tx: From Middle High German hopfe, from Old High German hopfo. Cognate with Dutch hop, English hop, French houblon.

noun:Hüfte.tx: From early modern German Hüfte (“hips”), plural of Huft (“hip”), itself with paragogic -t from Middle High German huf, from Old High German huf, from Proto-Germanic *hupiz, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱeu̯bh₂-. Cognate with Dutch heup, English hip, Danish hofte.

verb:hüpfen.tx: From Middle High German hüpfen, hupfen, from Old High German *hupfēn, from Proto-West Germanic *huppijan, from Proto-Germanic *huppijaną. Related with English hop and Dutch hippen.

adv:heute.tx: From Middle High German hiute, from Old High German hiutu, a contraction of earlier *hiu tagu, from Proto-West Germanic *hiu dagu, from Proto-Germanic *hinō dagō (“on this day”, from *hiz + *dagaz). Cognate with Old English hēodæġ (“today”) and Dutch heden (“today”). Compare German heuer from hiu (“in this”) + jāru (“year”).

noun:Hirse.tx: From Middle High German hirse, from Old High German hirso, from Proto-Germanic *hirsijô, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱer- (“to feed”).

noun:Halskette.tx: From Middle High German *halskette, from Old High German halsketinna (“neck shackle”). Equivalent to Hals (“neck”) + Kette (“chain”); cognate with Dutch halsketting.

noun:Harke.tx: Borrowed from Middle Low German harke. Cognate with Dutch hark. Compare also French herque (“metal rake”).

verb:holen.tx: From Middle High German holen, holn, from Old High German holōn, holēn (“to fetch, get, draw”), from Proto-West Germanic *holōn. Cognate with English haul.

noun:Hecht.tx: From Middle High German hechet, from Old High German hehhit, from Proto-Germanic *hakiþaz or *hakidaz, ultimately from the root of Haken (“hook”) (English hook). Cognate with Middle Dutch heket, Old Saxon hakth, *hakith, Old English hacod.

noun:Holunder.tx: With irregular stress shift (as in Wacholder, Forelle etc.) from Middle High German holunder, holunter, from Old High German holuntar, from Proto-West Germanic *holantr.

noun:Höcker.tx: Umlauted variant (16th c., perhaps from a plural and/or the adjective höckerig) of older Hocker (15th c.), itself an intensified form of Hoger, from Middle High German hoger, from Old High German hogar (12th c.). Related with Hügel and hoch.

noun:Haken.tx: From Middle High German hāke, from Old High German hāggo, hācko, hāko, from Proto-West Germanic *hākō, from Proto-Germanic *hēkô (see *hakô), from Proto-Indo-European *keg-, *keng- (“peg; hook”). Cognate with Old English hǣca (“hook, bolt”). One of the rare words with a long vowel followed by an original geminate, which was later simplified. Cognate with Dutch haak. Further related with Dutch …

adj:helle.tx: Regional variant of German hell. From Middle High German hellen, from the root of hell (“clear, bright”). Cognate with Dutch hel.

noun:Hornisse.tx: From Middle High German horniȥ, hornuȥ, from Old High German hurniȥ, hornuȥ, hornaȥ, from Proto-West Germanic *hurnutu. Cognate Dutch hoorn, hoorntje, English hornet.

noun:Huf.tx: From Old High German huof, from Proto-Germanic *hōfaz, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱoph₂ós. Cognate with Dutch hoef, West Frisian hoef, English hoof, Danish hov, and Swedish hov. Non-Germanic cognates include Russian копы́то (kopýto) and Sanskrit शफ (śapháḥ).

noun:Hass.tx: From Middle High German haȥ, from Old High German haȥ. Compare Dutch haat, English hate, Danish had; also Gothic 𐌷𐌰𐍄𐌹𐍃 (hatis), Old Norse hatr, Old English hete, Old Saxon heti.

noun:Harz.tx: From Middle High German harz, from Old High German harz(uh), from Proto-West Germanic *hart (“pitch, resin”).

noun:Hafer.tx: From Middle High German hafer, haber, hafere, habere, from Old High German habaro. The modern consonantism is Central German (compare Middle Low German haver, havere and modern German Low German Haver, Hafer). The Upper German cognate form Haber is now obsolete in standard usage.

noun:Haft.tx: From Middle High German haft, hafte (“captivity”), from Old High German haft, hafta. Immediately cognate with Middle Dutch hachte, Middle Low German hafte. Also related with Old English hæft, and further with Latin captus, Old Irish cacht.

noun:Halfter.tx: From Middle High German halfter, Old High German halftra (“halter”), from Proto-West Germanic *halftrijā.

noun:Hammel.tx: From Middle High German hamel, from Old High German hamal (“wether”, also an adjective “castrated”), from Proto-West Germanic *hamal, from Proto-Germanic *hamalaz (“mutilated”). Cognate with Dutch hamel.

noun:Huhn.tx: From Middle High German huon, from Old High German huon, from Proto-West Germanic *hōn. Compare Dutch hoen. See also German Henne.

noun:Härte.tx: From Middle High German herte, from Old High German hartī. By surface analysis, hart + -e.

noun:Haselnuss.tx: From Middle High German haselnuz, from Old High German hasalnuz. Analysable as Hasel + Nuss. Cognate with Dutch hazelnoot, English hazelnut.

noun:Hasel.tx: From Middle High German hasel, from Old High German hasal, from Proto-West Germanic *hasl.

noun:Hebel.tx: From Middle High German hebel, from Old High German *hebil, from Proto-West Germanic *habil, from Proto-Germanic *habilaz. By surface analysis, heben + -el. Cognate with Middle Low German hēvel, Middle English hevel, heveld.

noun:Hecke.tx: From Middle High German hecke, from Old High German hegga, from Proto-West Germanic *haggju, from Proto-Indo-European *kagʰyo-. Cognate with Dutch heg, English hedge.

noun:Hefe.tx: From Middle High German [Term?], from Old High German hevo, from Proto-West Germanic *habbjō.

verb:heften.tx: From Middle High German heften, from Old High German heften, from Proto-West Germanic *haftijan, from Proto-Germanic *haftijaną.

noun:Heiland.tx: From Middle High German heilant, from Old High German heilant. From the present participle of Old High German heilen. Calque of Latin salvātor.

noun:Heirat.tx: From Middle High German hīrāt, from Old High German hīrāt (“wedding; marriage”), from Proto-West Germanic *hīwarād. Cognate with Old English hīred (“family, household”). More at hird.

noun:Hilfe.tx: From Middle High German helfe, hilfe, from Old High German helfa, hilfa, from Proto-West Germanic [Term?], from Proto-Germanic *helpō, *hilpiz (“help”), from Proto-Germanic *helpaną (“to help”), from Proto-Indo-European *ḱelb-, *ḱelp- (“to help”). Among the three Middle High German variants helfe, hilfe, hülfe, the i-form is phonetically intermediate, but in Modern German the northern Hülfe was …

noun:Hemd.tx: From Middle High German hemde, hemede, from Old High German hemidi (“skin”), from Proto-West Germanic *hamiþi (“shirt”).

noun:Hengst.tx: Inherited from Middle High German hengest, from Old High German hengist, from Proto-West Germanic *hangist, from Proto-Germanic *hangistaz.

noun:Henkel.tx: From the root of henken (“to hang”) + -el.

noun:Henker.tx: From Middle High German henker, henkære, variant of henger, hengære, equivalent to henken + -er.

noun:Henne.tx: From Middle High German henne, from Old High German henna. Compare Dutch hen, English hen, Danish høne, Icelandic hæna. See also Huhn.

noun:Hering.tx: From Middle High German hærinc, herinc, from Old High German hārinc, herinc, from Proto-West Germanic *hāring, *haring, perhaps from a substrate language. The sense of "tent peg" is from to the visual similarity between the fish and long, silver-grey metal pegs. According to Pfeifer, this sense is attested by the late 19th century.

noun:Hermelin.tx: From Middle High German hermelīn, from Old High German harmilī, diminutive of harmo (“ermine”), from Proto-Germanic *harmô. Cognates outside Germanic only in Latvian sermulis and Lithuanian šarmuõ, šermuõ. The monophthong -i- in modern German (alongside obsolete Hermlein, Hermelein) as well as the final stress can be explained natively, as being from a non-diphthongising dialect on the one hand, …

verb:hetzen.tx: From Middle High German hetzen, from Old High German hezzen (“to pursue”), from Proto-West Germanic *hattjan, from Proto-Germanic *hatjaną (“to hunt down, pursue, persecute, attack”).

verb:heucheln.tx: Spread by Luther; origin unsettled. Probably from Middle Low German hüchelen (whence Danish hykle and Swedish hyckla), which may be akin to Old English hīewian. Older theories are based on Central German origin and relate the word to either hauchen (“to aspirate, to whisper”) or hocken (“to be bowed, to sit”). Compare Dutch huichelen (borrowed from German).

verb:hocken.tx: From Low German and Middle Low German hucken, from Proto-Germanic *hukkōną (“to squat”).

verb:heulen.tx: From Middle High German hiulen, from Old High German hūwilōn, from Proto-West Germanic *hūilōn.

noun:Hexe.tx: From Middle High German hecse, hesse, from Old High German hagazussa, from Proto-West Germanic *hagatussjā. Cognate with English hag.

noun:Hieb.tx: 15th century, derived from hieb (Middle High German hiew etc.), the older preterite of hauen.

noun:Hobel.tx: From Middle High German hovel, hobel, hubel, etc., from Old High German hovil, huobil. This is perhaps an early borrowing from Old Saxon because until the 14th century the word was chiefly Low German; compare Middle Low German hōvel. The wide variety of forms may also corroborate this. It seems uncertain whether the noun Hobel was derived from the verb hobeln or vice versa. Related with Hubbel …

noun:Hode.tx: From Old High German hodo, from Proto-Germanic *huþô.

noun:Höhle.tx: From Middle High German hüle, höle, from Old High German hulī, holī, analyzable as hol (“hollow”) + -ī (“-ness”) (modern hohl + -e), seemingly when a-umlaut was still active.

noun:Hülle.tx: From Middle High German hülle, from Old High German hulla, derived from the verb hullen (whence modern hüllen), from Proto-West Germanic *hulljan, from Proto-Germanic *huljaną. Related with English hull, though not immediately cognate.

noun:Hülse.tx: Middle High German hülse, from Old High German hulsa, *hulisa, from Proto-Germanic *hulisō, cognate with Proto-Germanic *huljaną and Proto-Germanic *helaną which yield hüllen (“to wrap”) and hehlen (“to hide”) resp. Related with English hull.

noun:Hüne.tx: From German Low German Hüne (“giant, hulk”), from Middle Low German hǖne (“hulk; Hun”), ultimately from the self-designation of the historic Huns. Compare Middle High German hiune, hūne (“Hun; Hungarian”), from Old High German hūn (“Hun”). The High German equivalent Heune became obsolete in Early Modern German and was superseded by the Latin-derived Ungar (“Hungarian”) and Hunne (“Hun”). However, …

noun:Hupe.tx: An onomatopoeic term derived from dialectal forms.

noun:Hürde.tx: From Middle High German hürde, genitive/dative of hurt, from Old High German hurd (“wickerwork”), from Proto-West Germanic *hurdi, *hurþi. The Old High German form (along with Old Saxon hurth) requires *þ. The byform hurt may have underlying *d, unless it is due to final devoicing (which is at any rate the case in Middle High German). The sports sense (late 19th c.) is a calque of English hurdle (since 1830s).

noun:Hohn.tx: From Middle High German hōn, from Old High German hōna, from Proto-Germanic *haunō, related with Proto-West Germanic *haunijan, << Proto-Germanic *haunijaną (“to shame; embarrass; humiliate”), whence English hean; see there.

noun:Habe.tx: From Middle High German habe, from Old High German haba, from Proto-West Germanic *habu.

noun:Hagebutte.tx: From Middle High German hagebutte, from Old High German haganbutta. By surface analysis, Hag (“hedge”) + -e- + Butte (“lump”) (dialectal), from Middle High German butte.

adv:hinten.tx: From Middle High German hinden(e), from Old High German hintana, from Proto-Germanic *hindanē. For the consonantism, see hinter.

adj:hager.tx: From Central Middle High German hager. The word is not originally present in Upper German. The standard literature is inconsistent on whether it was restricted to Central German or if it is also old in Low German (compare late Middle Low German hager). Further origin unknown. Kroonen (2013, 199) proposes descent from Proto-Germanic *hagra- (“slim”) and thence from a PIE -ro adjective from a root …

verb:hängen.tx: From a conflation of three interrelated verbs all originally meaning “to hang”, but varying in their transitivity and intransitivity: 1) Middle High German hāhen (transitive and intransitive), from Old High German hāhan (chiefly transitive [sic]), a strong verb with past forms hieng, gehangan, from Proto-West Germanic *hą̄han, from Proto-Germanic *hanhaną (intransitive). 2) Middle High German …

noun:Heil.tx: From Middle High German heil, from Old High German heil.

adj:heiser.tx: From Middle High German heiser (“rough, hoarse”), Old High German heisi (“hoarse”), from Proto-Germanic *haisaz. Cognate with Middle Dutch heersch, Old English hās, Dutch hees (“hoarse”), English hoarse, Old Norse háss.

adj:heiter.tx: From Middle High German heiter, from Old High German heitar, from Proto-West Germanic *haidr, from Proto-Germanic *haidraz. Compare Old Norse heiðr, Old English hādor and Sanskrit चित्र (citra, “bright, wonderful, multicolored”).

verb:heizen.tx: From Middle High German heizen, from Old High German heizen, from Proto-West Germanic *haitijan, from Proto-Germanic *haitijaną.

adj:hübsch.tx: From Middle High German hübesch (“courtly”), from the root of modern Hof (“court”). Cognate with Yiddish היפּש (hipsh). The term was probably borrowed into written Middle High German from Middle Dutch hovesch via West Central German, in which process the Central German -v- was hypercorrectly replaced with -b-. The somewhat younger Middle High German hövesch, in line with hof (“court”), led to …

verb:hemmen.tx: From Middle High German hemmen, from Old High German *hemmen (in Old High German gihemmen), from Proto-West Germanic *hammjan. Cognate with English hem, Swedish hämma, Icelandic hemja.

verb:hinken.tx: From Middle High German hinken, from Old High German hinkan, from Proto-West Germanic *hinkan, from Proto-Germanic *hinkaną.

adj:hohl.tx: From Middle High German and Old High German hol, from Proto-West Germanic *hol, from Proto-Germanic *hulaz (“hollow”).

adj:hinterfotzig.tx: This term comes from southern Germany, a compound word created from hinter (“behind”) and fotzig, the latter being derived from (regional) Fotze (“mouth, gob”). Therefore, the compound is an adjective for someone who is dishonest and likely to talk behind someone's back.

adv:hinterfotzig.tx: This term comes from southern Germany, a compound word created from hinter (“behind”) and fotzig, the latter being derived from (regional) Fotze (“mouth, gob”). Therefore, the compound is an adjective for someone who is dishonest and likely to talk behind someone's back.

verb:härten.tx: From Middle High German herten, from Old High German herten, from Proto-West Germanic *hardijan, from Proto-Germanic *hardijaną. By surface analysis, hart + -en.

verb:hallen.tx: From Middle High German hallen, from the root of Hall.

verb:heiligen.tx: From Middle High German heiligen, from Old High German heilagōn, from Proto-Germanic *hailagōną. Cognate with Dutch heiligen, English hallow.

adj:heftig.tx: From Middle High German heftec, from Old High German heiftig, probably from or related to Proto-West Germanic *haifsti (“struggle, conflict”). Compare Yiddish העפֿטיק (heftik). Probably influenced by Middle High German heifte (“impetuous”).

noun:Hanse.tx: From Middle High German hanse (“guild”), from Old High German hansa (“group; community; guild”), from Proto-West Germanic *hansu, from Proto-Germanic *hansō. The modern specification of these sense follows Middle Low German hanse (“guild; Hanseatic League”), which is itself an early borrowing from Middle High German.

noun:Huflattich.tx: From Old High German huoflatuhha. Equivalent to Huf (“hoof”) + Lattich (“lettuce”). So called because the leaves look similar to horsehooves; compare the English name.

noun:Harpune.tx: Borrowed from Dutch harpoen, which is usually considered a borrowing from French harpon (though this is contested).

noun:Hornhaut.tx: Compound of Horn "horn" (hard growth of keratin) + Haut "skin".

noun:Havanna.tx: Borrowed from Spanish La Habana, from Taíno Habaguanex, the native American chief (Cacique) who controlled the area.

noun:Homburg.tx: From Middle High German hœhe (“elevation”) + burc (“fortification, castle”). Equivalent to Höhenburg (“hill castle”).

noun:Haaresbreite.tx: From Haar (“hair”) + -es- + Breite (“breadth”), literally “breadth of a hair”.

noun:Hurrikan.tx: Borrowed from English hurricane. Doublet of Orkan.

noun:Hinterwäldler.tx: By surface analysis, hinter (“behind”) + Wald (“woods”) + -ler (agent suffix). Calque of English backwoodsman.

noun:Hurensohn.tx: From Hure (“whore”) + -n- + Sohn (“son”). Compare Dutch hoerenzoon, English whoreson.

adj:hässlich.tx: From Middle High German hezzelich, hazzelich, hazlich, hezlich, from Old High German hazlīh. Equivalent to Hass + -lich.

adj:hastig.tx: From Middle High German hastic, hastec. Analysable as Hast + -ig. Compare Middle Low German hastich (whence German Low German hastig, haastig).

noun:Hinterhalt.tx: From hinter + Halt in the sense of "place to hold position in", with ambushes being places where to attack from behind.

noun:Hängematte.tx: Alteration of Hamach, Hamaco, which is borrowed, probably via earlier Dutch hamak, from Spanish hamaca, from Taíno *hamaka. See English hammock for more. The Spanish form was reinterpreted as “hang-matt” by popular etymology both in German and in Dutch (see hangmat, also attested as hangmak). The modern German word is thus analysable as a compound of hängen + Matte. Such an adapted form is …

verb:horten.tx: From Middle High German *horten, horden, from Old High German *hortōn, from Proto-West Germanic *hoʀdōn (“to hoard”), equivalent to Hort (“shelter, refuge, haven”) + -en. Cognate with Old English hordian (whence English hoard).

noun:Hort.tx: From Middle High German hort, from Old High German hort, from Proto-Germanic *huzdą. Cognate with English hoard.

noun:Hindernis.tx: From Middle High German hindernisse. By surface analysis, hindern + -nis.

verb:hindern.tx: From Middle High German hindern, from Old High German hintaren. By surface analysis, hinter + -en.

noun:Hoffnung.tx: From hoffen + -ung. Cognate with Low German Huapnunge, Plautdietsch Hopninj, English hoping.

noun:Häkchen.tx: From Haken (“hook”) + -chen (diminutive suffix). Compare Dutch haakje, Czech háček.

adj:heikel.tx: Probably a dialectal variant of Middle Low German ēkel (“disgusting”), from which German Ekel (“loathing, disgust, fastidiousness”). A connection to Proto-Germanic *aikulaz (“fearful”) has been suggested for both words; compare Old English acol (“burdensome, troublesome”), English ache, Galician extern (“to vex”), Dutch akelig (“terrible”). Heikel seems to have arisen out of 16th century Upper …

noun:Hintern.tx: Generalised non-nominative form of Hinterer (“that which is back, backside”), a nominalisation of the adjective hinterer (“back, further to the back”).

noun:Hokuspokus.tx: Borrowed from English hocus-pocus, and this a pseudo-Latinism; see that entry for more.

noun:Homöopathie.tx: Coined in 1796 by German physician Samuel Hahnemann from Ancient Greek ὅμοιος (hómoios, “like, resembling”) + πάθος (páthos, “pain”), homöo- + -pathie.

noun:Humanismus.tx: Coined by German philosopher and theologian Friedrich Immanuel Niethammer in 1808.

noun:Heißluftballon.tx: From heiß (“hot”) + Luft (“air”) + Ballon (“balloon”) or alternatively Heißluft (“hot air”) + Ballon (“balloon”). Compare Luftballon.

verb:hageln.tx: From Middle High German hagelen, synchronically analyzable as Hagel (“hail”) + -n. Compare Dutch hagelen, English hail (verb).

noun:Haushalt.tx: Cognate with English household, Middle Low German hūsholt, Dutch huishouden (earlier huishold). By surface analysis, Haus (“house”) + halten (“to hold”).

noun:Hoden.tx: From Middle High German hōde, from Old High German hōdo, from Proto-West Germanic *huþō. The vowel of the Old High German is usually reconstructed as long, but some modern dialects require original shortness, as does apparently Old Frisian hothan, the only Germanic cognate. Perhaps ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *(s)kewH- (“cover”) and then cognate with Welsh cwd (“scrotum”), Ancient Greek …

noun:Horst.tx: From Middle High German hurst, from Old High German hurst, from Proto-West Germanic *hursti. The modern vowel is Central and Low German (compare Middle Low German horst). Cognate to Dutch horst, English hurst.

noun:Hufeisen.tx: From Middle High German huofīsen, from Old High German huofīsan; equivalent to Huf (“hoof”) + Eisen (“iron”).

adj:hektisch.tx: Via Old French from Late Latin hecticus (“febrile”), from Ancient Greek ἑκτικός (hektikós, “habitual”).

verb:hamstern.tx: Hamster (“hamster”) + -en. The hamster is said to hoard food; compare English squirrel, Polish chomikować.

noun:Hirte.tx: From Middle High German hirt, hirte, from Old High German hirt, hirti, from Proto-West Germanic *hirdī, from Proto-Germanic *hirdijaz.

adj:heimlich.tx: From Middle High German heimlich, heimelich, from Old High German heimilīh, from Proto-West Germanic *haimalīk. Equivalent to Heim + -lich.

adj:hungrig.tx: From Proto-Germanic *hungragaz, *hungrugaz (“hungry”). By surface analysis, Hunger + -ig. Compare Dutch hongerig, English hungry.

noun:Homophobie.tx: Borrowed from English homophobia. By surface analysis, homo- + -phobie

noun:Haschee.tx: Borrowed from French haschée, a now obsolete spelling of hachée.

noun:Handwerk.tx: From Middle High German hantwerc, from Old High German hantwerc, hantwerch, from Proto-Germanic *handuwerką; equivalent to Hand + Werk. More at handiwork.

noun:Hugenotte.tx: From French huguenot. Possibly a doublet of Eidgenosse.

verb:heiraten.tx: From Middle High German hīrāten, which is derived from Middle High German hīrāt (“marriage”), whence German Heirat (“marriage”).

adj:höflich.tx: From Middle High German hovelich (“in accordance with the customs of the court”), which is derived from Middle High German hof, from Old High German hof, from Proto-West Germanic *hof, from Proto-Germanic *hufą. By surface analysis, Hof + -lich. In a similar way is Old French cortois derived from cort.

noun:Hyazinthe.tx: 16th century, as Hyacinthus m from Latin hyacinthus, which see for more. The feminine in -e (17th c.) is a backformation from the plural and/or influenced by French hyacinthe.

noun:Hibiskus.tx: 19th century, from Late Latin hibīscus, whence also older Eibisch.

adj:hysterisch.tx: 18th century, from Latin hyster(icus) + -isch, perhaps after French hystérique (16th c.).

noun:Handtuch.tx: From Middle High German hanttuoch, from Old High German hanttuoh. By surface analysis, Hand (“hand”) + Tuch (“cloth”).

noun:Hypnose.tx: From modern scholarly Ancient Greek ὕπνωσις (húpnōsis), which formation closes the derivational gap between the ancient word ὑπνόω (hupnóō, “I put to sleep”) and ὑπνωτικός (hupnōtikós, “sleep-inducing, soporific”).

verb:heilen.tx: From Middle High German heilen, from Old High German heilen, from Proto-West Germanic *hailijan (“to heal, make whole, save”). See there for more cognates.

noun:Heute.tx: From Middle High German hiute, from Old High German hiutu, hiuto (“today”), a contraction of hiu tagu (literally “(on) this day”), from Proto-West Germanic *hiu dagu, from Proto-Germanic *hinō dagō (from *hiz+*dagaz (“on this day”)); similar to other constructions in Old High German (e.g. hiuro < *hiu jāru (“(in) this year”), see Heuer). Cognates Cognate with Old Dutch hiudo (> Dutch heden …

adj:heidnisch.tx: Inherited from Middle High German heidenisch, from Old High German heidanisc. By surface analysis, Heide(n) + -isch.

noun:Hausdurchsuchung.tx: Extended form of earlier Haussuchung. Analyzable as Haus (“house”) + Durchsuchung (“search”).

noun:Häresie.tx: From Medieval Latin haeresis, from Ancient Greek αἵρεσις (haíresis, “taking, receiving; choice”).

verb:herunterladen.tx: herunter- + laden, calque of English download.

verb:horchen.tx: An originally Central German word, from northern Middle High German horchen, hōrchen, from late Old High German hōrechen, probably from original Proto-West Germanic *hauʀukōn derived from Proto-West Germanic *hauʀijan whence German hören.

adv:heran.tx: From her + an; compare English hereon.

noun:Horoskop.tx: From Latin horoscopium, from Ancient Greek ὡροσκοπεῖον (hōroskopeîon).

noun:Heimlichkeit.tx: Middle High German heimlīchkeit, by surface analysis, heimlich + -keit.

adv:hochkant.tx: By surface analysis, hoch (“high”) + Kante (“edge”). Compare Swedish på högkant.

adj:hochkant.tx: By surface analysis, hoch (“high”) + Kante (“edge”). Compare Swedish på högkant.

noun:Hinkelstein.tx: Originally a Rhine Franconian dialect word denoting a number of menhirs in Hesse. Generalised and standardised in the 19th century. The form is analysable as Hinkel (“chicken”) + Stein (“stone”). Likely from of an underlying Hünenstein, from Middle High German hiune (“giant”, literally “Hun”); compare modern German Hüne. This would first have been corrupted to Hühnerstein, and then further to the …

adv:heuer.tx: From Middle High German hiure, from Old High German hiuro, hiuru, from hiu (“in this”) + jāru (“year”). Compare German heute from Old High German hiu tagu ("this day").

noun:Heuer.tx: From Middle Low German hūre, from Old Saxon huria (“hire”). Cognate to Dutch huur.

verb:heuern.tx: Borrowed from Middle Low German hüren, from Proto-West Germanic *hūʀijan.

verb:hecken.tx: From Middle High German hecken, from Proto-Germanic *hakjaną. Cognate with English hatch, Swedish häcka.

noun:Huld.tx: From Middle High German hulde, hülde, from Old High German huldī (“friendliness”), from Proto-West Germanic *hulþī. Cognate to Dutch hulde, Icelandic hylli.

noun:Häuptling.tx: From Old Frisian hāvdling (“high member of the nobility”), probably via Middle Low German [Term?]. By surface analysis, Haupt + -ling. The umlaut is probably due to the northern origin of the word and derives from the earlier Central German variant Häupt, though it might also be due to analogy with other words in -ling. The word was first adopted in the sense of "patriarch, family leader", but …

noun:Hüttenkäse.tx: From Hütte (“hut, cottage”) + -n- + Käse (“cheese”), a calque of English cottage cheese. Trademarked by the dairy company Hochland in 1964, though isolated earlier uses are attested.

noun:Hintergrund.tx: hinter- + Grund, originally in the context of stage plays, possibly under the influence of English background.

noun:Handschrift.tx: Hand (“hand”) + Schrift (“script, writing”). First attested in the 15th century, compare hantschrift (15th century). Compare Dutch handschrift.

noun:Hantel.tx: 19th century, from an infrequent Low German dialect word, which was spread (like several others) by Jahn. Pertaining to Hand (“hand”).

verb:hissen.tx: 16th century, from Middle Low German hissen, of unknown origin. Possibly the same word as Middle Low German hissen, hitzen, Middle Dutch hissen (modern Dutch ophitsen), Old French hicier, all meaning “to set hounds on”. These can be compared to Proto-Germanic *hatjaną (whence High German hetzen), but the phonetics are highly problematic. Therefore the group is usually considered imitative, …

noun:Haftung.tx: From Middle High German haftunge, from Old High German haftunga. By surface analysis, haften (“to be liable, to stick”) + -ung (“-ing”).

noun:Hochmut.tx: From Middle High German hōchmuot, from Old High German hōhmuot. Equivalent to hoch + Mut. Cognate with Dutch hoogmoed and Old English hēahmōdnes.

adj:hochmütig.tx: From Middle High German hōchmüetic, from Old High German hōhmuotīg. By surface analysis, Hochmut + -ig.

adj:heutig.tx: From Middle High German hiutec, from Old High German hiutīg, derived from hiutu (“today”). Analyzable as heute + -ig.

noun:Hypothek.tx: Borrowed from Latin hypothēca (“pledge, mortgage”), from Ancient Greek ὑποθήκη (hupothḗkē, “warning, pledge”).

adj:hilfreich.tx: Inherited from Middle High German hëlferîche. By surface analysis, Hilfe + -reich.

verb:herausfinden.tx: From heraus- + finden. Compare English find out.

intj:hurra.tx: Probably from Middle High German hurrā, an imperative from hurren (“to move quickly”), from Proto-Germanic *hurzaną (“to rush”), from Proto-Indo-European *ḱers- (“to run”).

intj:heureka.tx: Borrowed from Ancient Greek εὕρηκα (heúrēka, “I have found”).

noun:Heiligkeit.tx: heilig + -keit or Middle High German heilecheit, heilicheit (heilekeit, heilikeit, heilichait)

noun:Hormon.tx: From Ancient Greek ὁρμῶν (hormôn), present participle of ὁρμάω (hormáō, “to set in motion, to urge on”).

noun:Heilbutt.tx: Borrowed from German Low German Helbutt (with variants). By surface analysis, heil + Butt.

noun:Herkunft.tx: her- + kunft, from kommen. The second element's spelling development is similar to Abkunft.

noun:Halbinsel.tx: halb (“half”) + Insel (“island”), a calque of Latin paenīnsula. Compare Danish halvø, Low German Halfinsel, Norwegian Bokmål halvøy, Swedish halvö, Yiddish האַלבאינדזל (halbindzl)

noun:Hahnrei.tx: Borrowed from Middle Low German hanenrey. The word is also attested in Middle High German [Term?], but it was rare and the later spread was without doubt based on Low German. The original sense seems to have been “capon”, that is a castrated cock. Further etymology unsettled. Compare Swedish hanrej, from the same source.

noun:Hete.tx: Clipping of hetero or heterosexuell (“heterosexual”), modeled after Homo, as well as feminine clippings in -e, hence the gender.

noun:Hyäne.tx: Borrowed from Latin hyaena, from Ancient Greek ὕαινα (húaina). At first also hientier (15th century). According to Pliny, precious stones called hyaenia are won from hyena eyes, whence Middle High German hiennia (“kind of gem”), perhaps already Old High German hiena (“handle made of gemstone”).

noun:Hypochonder.tx: Back-formation from hypochondrisch, possibly on the model of French hypocondre.

noun:Hain.tx: A Central German form spread by Luther, from Middle High German hagen, from Old High German hagan. Compare the closely related Hag.

noun:Hainbuche.tx: From Middle High German hagenbuoche, from Old High German haganbuohha, from hagan (“hawthorn, hedge”) and buohha (“beech”).

noun:Hermeneutik.tx: Borrowed from Ancient Greek ἑρμηνευτική (τέχνη) (hermēneutikḗ (tékhnē), “art of interpretation”), from ἑρμηνεύειν (hermēneúein, “to explain, to interpret”).

verb:halsen.tx: From Middle High German halsen, from Old High German halsôn, from Proto-West Germanic *halsijan, from Proto-Germanic *halsijaną.

noun:Häme.tx: Backformation from hämisch. First attested in the 1960s, probably slightly older in speech.

adj:hauptsächlich.tx: From Hauptsache + -lich, equivalent to haupt- + Sache + -lich

adv:hauptsächlich.tx: From Hauptsache + -lich, equivalent to haupt- + Sache + -lich

noun:Heizung.tx: heizen (“to heat”) + -ung (nominal suffix to form nouns from verbs)

adj:hartnäckig.tx: Bahuvrīhi compound of hart (“hard”) + Nacken (“neck”) + -ig (adjective suffix), literally “one with a hard, inflexible neck”.

noun:Häfen.tx: See the etymology of the corresponding lemma form.

noun:Hinterland.tx: From hinter (“behind”) + Land (“land”). First attested in the 15th century, in current use since the later 19th century.

noun:Hypophyse.tx: From Ancient Greek ὑπόφυσις (hupóphusis, “attachment underneath”), from ὑπο- (hupo-, “under”) + φύσις (phúsis, “nature”), from φύω (phúō, “to bring forth”).

noun:Hausmann.tx: From Middle High German hūsman (“householder, resident, tenant, keeper”), from Old High German hūsman (“villein, domestic servant, resident”), from Proto-West Germanic *hūsamann. Equivalent to Haus + Mann.

noun:Heia.tx: Chiefly Central German word attested since the 18th century. Related to common lullaby verses like heia popeia. This is probably of mere interjectional origin, though some have ventured to derive it from Proto-Indo-European *ḱey- (“to lie down”), in which case it would be related with Heirat. The late attestation is only a weak counterargument in such a childish word; nevertheless the relation …

verb:hieven.tx: Ca. 1800, in nautical parlance, thus perhaps through Low German, eventually from English heave, from Middle English heven, from Old English hebban, from Proto-West Germanic *habbjan. Doublet of heben and kapieren.

noun:Herrschaft.tx: From hehr + -schaft, with the first element remodelled after Herr since at least MHG; cf. the same development in herrlich and herrschen. Compare Dutch heerschappij and Czech panstvo.

verb:herrschen.tx: From Middle High German hērschen, hērsen, from Old High German hērrisōn, hērisōn, from Proto-West Germanic *hairisōn (“to be strong, dominate”); ultimately from the root of hehr (“holy, sublime”), with the first element remodelled after Herr already during MHG; cf. the same development in herrlich and Herrschaft.

noun:Harnisch.tx: From Middle High German harnasch, harnisch, from Old French hernois. Usually derived from an Old Norse *hernest (“army equipment”), from herr (“army”) + nest (“provisions”) (from Proto-Germanic *nesaną (“to heal, recover”)), the former related with German Heer. A less likely derivation is from Old Breton hoiarn (“iron”), from Proto-Brythonic *hijarn, from Proto-Celtic *īsarnom, related with …

verb:harren.tx: From Middle High German harren, further origin is unclear. Popularised by Luther. Perhaps borrowed from Middle Low German harren, harden (“to wait, await”), from Old Saxon *hardōn (“to become hard, harden, be steadfast, await”), from Proto-West Germanic *hardēn (“to become hard, endure, wait, persevere”), related to Old High German hartēn (“to harden, await, endure, be steadfast”). Cognate with …

noun:Heldentenor.tx: Helden + Tenor, from Held (“hero”); Literally, “hero tenor”

noun:Händel.tx: Considered to be the plural of Handel m

noun:Hader.tx: From Middle High German hader, from Old High German hadu- (“battle”), from Proto-West Germanic *haþu. Akin to Old English *heaþu. Other Indo-European cognates include Old Norse hǫð/ hǫðr (“battle”)/ Hǫðr, Irish cath (“battle”), Proto-Slavic *kotera / *kotora (“quarrel, fight”), Old Church Slavonic котора (kotora), and Sanskrit शत्रु (śatru, “foe”).

noun:Halbgott.tx: From Middle High German *halpgot, from Old High German halbgot. Equivalent to halb + Gott.

noun:Herzogtum.tx: F>Inherited from Middle High German herzog(en)tuom. Equivalent to Herzog + -tum.

noun:Hufe.tx: From Middle High German hūfe, hūve, a northern byform of huobe, from Old High German huoba (also hōva, huova), from Proto-Germanic *hōbō. The v-form is expected only in Central Franconian, but irregularly established itself also in East Central German, possibly by association with hof (“estate, farmstead”). It was reinforced by Middle Low German hôve, from Old Saxon hōva. Further cognate with Dutch hoeve.

adv:hinauf.tx: From Middle High German hinūf, from Old High German hinūf, hinaūf. By surface analysis, hin + auf.

verb:huldigen.tx: From Middle High German huldigen. By surface analysis, Huld + -igen.

adv:herüber.tx: From Middle High German herüber. Equivalent to her- + über.

noun:Haspel.tx: From Middle High German haspel, from Old High German haspil, from Proto-West Germanic *haspilaz, from Proto-Germanic *haspulaz, diminutive of Proto-Germanic *haspijǭ (“clasp; hasp; reel”). More at hasp.

noun:Hellebarde.tx: From Middle High German helle(n)barte, from older helmbarte, from helm (“stalk”) + barte (“axe”). The modern -d- is Central and Low German (compare Middle Low German hēlenbārde) and/or influenced by French hallebarde, itself from the Middle High German. The stress pattern, too, may hint at French influence, though stress shifts in compound words also occur natively.

noun:Haubitze.tx: Borrowed during the Hussite Wars (early 15th c.) from Old Czech haufnicě (modern Czech houfnice). Compare modern German Haufen, modern Czech houf (“flock, crowd”). Early German forms were huffnitze, hauffenicz. The current form with -b- appears around 1700.

verb:hochladen.tx: From hoch + laden, a calque of English upload.

noun:Häher.tx: From Middle High German hëher, from Old High German hëhara, hëhera, Proto-Germanic *hihurō, *skihurō (compare Low German Heger, dialectal English heighaw (“woodpecker, popinjay”), Norwegian skjor), from Proto-Indo-European *kik- (compare Proto-West Germanic *higurō, Lithuanian kḗkštas, Greek κίσσα (kíssa), Sanskrit किकिदीवि (kikidīvί, “blue jay”)).

verb:hinlegen.tx: From Middle High German hinlegen, from Old High German hinaleggen. Equivalent to hin- + legen.

noun:Hauptmann.tx: From Middle High German houbetman (“leader; captain, head of a group”), from Old High German houbitman, from Proto-West Germanic *haubidamann. Cognate with Low German Hööftmann, Dutch hoofdman, and Old English hēafodmann. Equivalent to haupt- (“chief, head”) + Mann (“man”). Doublet of Hetman (via Polish hetman).

noun:Herrgott.tx: From Middle High German hērre got, hërre got, equivalent to Herr (“Lord”) + Gott (“God”).

intj:Herrgott.tx: From Middle High German hērre got, hërre got, equivalent to Herr (“Lord”) + Gott (“God”).

noun:Handschlag.tx: From Middle High German hantslac, from Old High German hantslac, hantslag, hantaslag, from Proto-West Germanic *handuslagi, from Proto-Germanic *handuslagiz. Equivalent to Hand (“hand”) + Schlag (“blow, hit”). Cognate with Dutch handslag, Danish håndslag, Swedish handslag.

noun:Hoheit.tx: From Middle High German hôchheit; equivalent to Hoch + -heit.

noun:Hundstage.tx: Hund (“dog”) + Tag (“day”), a calque of Latin dies caniculares (“dog days”). See dog days for more information.

noun:Hauptsache.tx: From Middle High German houbetsache, equivalent to haupt- + Sache. Cognate with Middle Low German hȫvetsāke.

conj:Hauptsache.tx: From Middle High German houbetsache, equivalent to haupt- + Sache. Cognate with Middle Low German hȫvetsāke.

noun:Hiragana.tx: From Japanese 平(ひら)仮(が)名(な) (hiragana).

noun:Haiku.tx: Borrowed from Japanese 俳(はい)句(く) (haiku) from Middle Chinese 俳 (bɛj, “paralleled [writing]”) + 句 (kjù, “line”).

noun:Hentai.tx: Borrowed from English hentai, and this a pseudo-Japonism derived from Japanese 変態(へんたい) (hentai); see that entry for more.

verb:hausen.tx: From Middle High German hūsen, from Old High German hūsōn, from Proto-Germanic *hūsōną. Cognate with Dutch huizen, Low German husen, English house, Faroese húsa.

verb:hämmern.tx: From Middle High German hemern, hemeren, from Old High German *hemeren, *hemerren, *hemerien, from Old High German *hamarjaną, *hamarōną (“to hammer”), related to the Proto-Germanic noun *hamaraz. Cognate with Middle Low German hēmeren, German Low German hamern (“to hammer”), Dutch hameren (“to hammer”), English hammer (“to hammer”), Danish hamre (“to hammer”), Swedish hamra (“to hammer”).

noun:Hausen.tx: From Middle High German hūse, from Old High German hūso, from Proto-West Germanic *hūsō (“sturgeon”).

noun:Hacienda.tx: Borrowed from Spanish hacienda, from Latin facienda.

noun:Harm.tx: From Middle High German harm, from Old High German harm, from Proto-Germanic *harmaz (“harm; shame; pain”).

adv:herum.tx: From Middle High German her umbe, equivalent to modern her (“hither”) + um (“about”).

adv:hinüber.tx: From Middle High German hinüber. Equivalent to hin- + über.

noun:Halo.tx: Borrowed from Medieval Latin halo, from accusative of Latin halos, from Ancient Greek ἅλως (hálōs, “disk of the sun or moon; ring of light around the sun or moon; threshing floor with its surrounding threshold; disk of a shield”).

noun:Holm.tx: Probably from Middle Low German holm (“girt”), from Old Saxon *helma, from Proto-West Germanic *helmō, which pertains to the Germanic root *helmô (compare English helm). Older theories derive it from the plural of dialectal Hulbe (“beam”) with -ben → -m (a rather common development in German). This seems less likely, particularly since Holm was spread by Jahn, who introduced several Low German …

noun:Hochburg.tx: Calque of Ancient Greek ἀκρόπολις (akrópolis), from hoch + Burg.

noun:Haff.tx: Ca. 1800, from Low German Haff, from Middle Low German haf, from Old Saxon *haf, from Proto-West Germanic *hab, from Proto-Germanic *habą (“heaving sea”). Cognate with Old English hæf and Danish hav.

adj:herrlich.tx: From Middle High German hērlich, from Old High German hērlīh, equivalent to hehr (“sublime, noble”) + -lich, with the first element remodelled after Herr already during OHG; cf. the same development in Herrschaft and herrschen. Cognate with Dutch heerlijk (“delicious, lovely, delightful”), Swedish härlig. More at hoar, -ly.

adj:hehr.tx: From Middle High German hēr, hēre, from Old High German hēr (“noble, austere, venerable, aged”), from Proto-West Germanic *hair, from Proto-Germanic *hairaz (“grey, hoary”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)ḱeh₃i-, extension of *(s)ḱeh₃- (“grey”). Cognate with English hoar (“grey”) and hare (“grey, hoary, venerable”), modern German Herr.

noun:Havarie.tx: Via Middle Low German haverye from early modern Dutch haverij (modern averij), from French avarie, Italian avaria, from Arabic عَوَارِيَّة (ʕawāriyya). Compare contemporary Dutch averij. Doublet of average.

noun:Himmelskörper.tx: Compound of Himmel (“sky, heaven”) + -s- + Körper (“body”). Compare English celestial body, Swedish himlakropp, Italian corpo celeste.

adj:halsstarrig.tx: From Hals + starr + -ig. Calque of Hebrew קשה ערף (Exodus 33). A biblical term similar to Swedish hårdnackad, Ancient Greek σκληροτράχηλος (sklērotrákhēlos), Russian жестоковыйный (žestokovyjnyj) etc.

verb:herkommen.tx: From Middle High German herkomen, from Old High German heraqueman. Equivalent to her + kommen.

noun:Hautärztin.tx: Haut (“skin”) + Ärztin (“physician”) or rather Hautarzt + -in with umlaut

verb:hergehen.tx: From the compounding of the prefix her and gehen.

verb:hochfliegen.tx: From the compounding of hoch (“up”) and fliegen (“to fly”), from Old High German fliogan (“to fly”), from Proto-Germanic *fleuganą (“to fly”).

noun:Hepatitis.tx: From Latin hēpatītis, from hēpar (“liver”), from Ancient Greek ἧπαρ (hêpar, “liver”).

noun:Herrlichkeit.tx: From Middle High German hērlīcheit. By surface analysis, herrlich + -keit.

noun:Hausärztin.tx: Hausarzt (“family doctor”) + -in or Haus (“house”) + Ärztin (“female doctor”)

verb:humpeln.tx: Borrowed from German Low German [Term?], from Middle Low German *humpelen (attested in the nominalization humpeler). Compare Dutch hompelen, which, according to Van Neen & Van der Sijs, is of imitative origin, akin to huppen, English hop, etc.

verb:häufen.tx: From Middle High German houfen, hūfen, from Old High German hūfōn, from hūfo (“a heap”), from Proto-Germanic *haupaz, whence English heap.

verb:hegen.tx: From Middle High German hegen, from Old High German heggan (“surrounded by a fence”), ultimately from the root of archaic Hag (“hedge”) and modern Gehege (“enclosure”).

noun:Hegen.tx: verbal noun of hegen (“to cherish, care for”)

verb:hüllen.tx: From Middle High German hüllen, from Old High German hullen, hullan, from Proto-West Germanic *hulljan, from Proto-Germanic *huljaną.

verb:handhaben.tx: From Middle High German hanthaben (1349). The earliest sense is “to keep, protect, maintain”, hence eventually a loan translation of Old French maintenir and/or Latin manūtenēre. The possible French origin and the earlier attestation of Middle Dutch hanthaven (1286) and Middle Low German handhafen (1330) suggest that the word may have been borrowed through these. The Germanic formation must be …

verb:holpern.tx: Early New High German, of unclear origin, possibly of imitative origin (lautmalend). However, compare Lithuanian klupt (“to bend or move quickly, jolt, stumble, fall upon”) and klùpti, klū́poti (“to kneel”).

noun:Hausfriedensbruch.tx: From Hausfriede + -ns- + Bruch, literally “breach of domestic peace”. Compare Dutch huisvredebreuk.

noun:Hartung.tx: Derived from hart (“hard”) from the ground being frozen and hard.

adj:harzig.tx: From late Middle High German harzig, equivalent to Harz (“resin”) + -ig.

verb:herausbringen.tx: From Middle High German herūzbringen. Equivalent to heraus- + bringen.

noun:Heller.tx: From the name of the city of Hall am Kocher (today Schwäbisch Hall).

adj:häuslich.tx: From Middle High German hiuslīche, hiuslīchen, hūslīche. Equivalent to Haus + -lich.

adv:hinzu.tx: From Middle High German hin zū, from hin + zū.

noun:Halstuch.tx: From Middle High German halstuoch, from Old High German halstuoh. Equivalent to Hals + Tuch. Cognates include Dutch halsdoek.

noun:Humpen.tx: 16th century, of uncertain origin. Cognate with Middle Low German hump (“heap, lump”), Dutch homp (“chunk, gobbet”), English hump, all possibly from a Proto-West Germanic *hump. Within High German it was originally restricted to the colonial dialects (i.e. East Central German), which might suggest a borrowing from the Middle Low German form (though the -mp- is regular). As none of the Germanic …

adv:herab.tx: From Middle High German her (“to here”) + ab, abe (“off, down”), equivalent to her- + ab.

adj:heimisch.tx: From Middle High German heimisch, from Old High German heimisk; by surface analysis, Heim + -isch.

pron:höchstselbst.tx: From the superlative of hoch + selbst.

verb:hehlen.tx: From Middle High German heln, from Old High German helan, from Proto-West Germanic *helan, from Proto-Germanic *helaną.

verb:heischen.tx: From Middle High German heischen, eischen, from Old High German eiscōn, from Proto-West Germanic *aiskōn (“to ask, demand”).

verb:hinnehmen.tx: From Middle High German hinnëmen, from Old High German hinanëman. Equivalent to hin- + nehmen.

adv:halbwegs.tx: From halb + Weg + -s (adverbial suffix). Compare English halfway, Dutch halfweg.

adj:harsch.tx: From Low German and Middle Low German harsch, from Proto-Germanic *harskaz; see also Russian короста (korosta, “to itch”), Old Church Slavonic краста (krasta), Lithuanian karsiu (“to comb”). Compare English harsh, which is also borrowed from Middle Low German.

adv:harsch.tx: From Low German and Middle Low German harsch, from Proto-Germanic *harskaz; see also Russian короста (korosta, “to itch”), Old Church Slavonic краста (krasta), Lithuanian karsiu (“to comb”). Compare English harsh, which is also borrowed from Middle Low German.

noun:Halbzeit.tx: From halb (“half”) + Zeit (“time”), after English half-time.

noun:Handvoll.tx: From Middle High German hantvol, hantfol, from Old High German hantfol, from Proto-Germanic *handufulliz, *handufullō, equivalent to Hand + voll. Cognate with Dutch handvol, English handful, Icelandic handfylli.

adj:hinterlistig.tx: From Middle High German hinderlistic, hinderlistec, from Old High German hintarlistīg. Equivalent to hinter- + listig.

noun:Hüter.tx: From Middle High German hüetære, from Old High German huotâri, huoteri. By surface analysis, hüten (“to watch”) + -er (agent noun suffix).

noun:Hubbel.tx: From Middle High German hübel, from Old High German hubil. Many variants exist in Central German and German Low German. According to Pokorny, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *kew- (“to bend; a bend, joint”). Cognate with Dutch hobbel. Related to Middle High German hübel (“hill”) and Dutch heuvel.

adv:hinnen.tx: Middle High German hinnen (cp. hinne, hinnān)

noun:Hausherr.tx: From Middle High German hūsherre, from Old High German hūshērro, hūshēriro. Equivalent to Haus (“house”) + Herr (“master, lord”).

noun:Hofrat.tx: From Hof (“courtyard, court; royal court”) + Rat (“council; councilor”).

verb:hecheln.tx: An onomatopoeic word liable to alteration and variation. Formally iterative of obsolete hechen, heichen (“to pant”), a chiefly Central and Low German word; compare Middle Low German hīgen, heigen, hēgen (“to pant”), from or related with Proto-West Germanic *hīgōn (whence Dutch hijgen, English hie). Another obsolete variant German hechzen is derived from or reinterpreted as the interjection hach! …

noun:Heiligtum.tx: From Middle High German heilectuom, from Old High German heiligtuom. Equivalent to heilig + -tum. Cognate with English halidom

verb:heimzahlen.tx: From heim- (“home”) + zahlen (“pay”). Compare English pay home.
