verb:hantieren.tx: From Middle High German hantieren, which is borrowed—probably via Middle Low German—from Middle Dutch hanteren, itself from Old French hanter (“to frequent someone”). The Old French word is usually traced back Old Norse heimta (“to bring home”). The semantic development in German is based on popular association with Hand (“hand”) (already in Middle Dutch).

noun:Happs.tx: Variant of Happen with German Low German nominal -s.

adj:happig.tx: Originally, "greedy, excessive, difficult to swallow", 18th-century creation apparently from happ, imitative of the sound of snapping. Possibly borrowed from German Low German; compare Low German happen, happen (“to snap, to devour”). Related to German Happen (“bite-sized piece, bite”).

adj:heilfroh.tx: Originally heil froh (literally “very glad, totally glad”) (compare Dutch heel blij). This use of heil is not generally part of standard German, but is normal in German Low German and some dialects of Central German.

verb:hoppeln.tx: From Middle High German hoppeln, iterative form of hoppen. The latter is formally a Low German and Central German variant of hüpfen (“to hop”) (from Middle High German hüpfen or hupfen; it is also present, however, in Alemannic dialects (where it may be borrowed from the North or formed independently through onomatopoeia). By surface analysis, hoppen + -eln.

verb:hopsen.tx: From Middle High German *hopzen, from Old High German hopfezzen, hophezzen, hoppezzen, hoppazzen, from Proto-West Germanic *hoppattjan. Cognate with Old English hoppettan.

adv:huckepack.tx: Borrowed from Low German Huckeback, as in enen up’n Huckeback nömen (literally “to take someone on one’s piggyback”). The first component is cognate with German Hucke (“load, burden”) or a related verb hucken (“to carry a load”). The second component is from Middle Low German bak (“back”) by the consensus of the etymological standard literature. The component -back was associated with Pack …

noun:Hanseat.tx: Hanse + -at. The cookies are so called because they are coloured like the Hanseatic flag.

pt: dated form of hier
adv:hienieden.tx: From hie (“dated form of hier”) + nieden (“down”) (obsolete).

noun:Halter.tx: From Middle High German haltære (shepherd), from Old High German haltāri (saviour). See Halfter.

verb:hüten.tx: From Middle High German hüeten, Old High German huoten (“to watch, take care”), from Proto-West Germanic *hōdijan, see there for further etymology. Cognate with Old Saxon hōdian, Old English hēdan, Dutch hoeden, English heed.

verb:hingehen.tx: From Middle High German hingān, from Old High German hinagān. Equivalent to hin- + gehen.

noun:Hornung.tx: From Middle High German hornunc, from Old High German hornung (“bastard”) (viz.); one of Charlemagne's proposed names for reformed calendar months with limited success, according to Einhard. The apparent semantic connection has been postulated to February being the "odd one out" amongst months (shortest and changing dates), hence the "bastard month". Compare Pennsylvania German Hanning, Old …

verb:herzen.tx: From Middle High German hërzen. Equivalent to Herz (“heart”) + -en.

noun:Honk.tx: Uncertain. Apparently not attested before the 21st century. One theory traces it back to English honky (“white person”), but this word is little known in Germany and the semantics are hardly satisfactory. Somewhat more plausible seems the derivation from a humorous military acronym for Hauptschüler ohne nennenswerte Kenntnisse (HonK), roughly referring to a “recruit with lesser education and no …

noun:Heimcomputer.tx: From Heim + Computer, calque of English home computer.

adj:handzahm.tx: From Middle High German *hantzam, from Old High German hantzām, hantzam, from Proto-West Germanic *handutam, equivalent to Hand (“hand”) + zahm (“tame”). Compare English handtame.

noun:Hemmschuh.tx: From hemmen (“to inhibit, to obstruct”) + Schuh (“shoe”).

noun:Haussuchung.tx: By surface analysis, Haus (“house”) + suchen (“to search”) + -ung (“-ing”). Formally from a rare Middle High German hūssuochunge, which is only attested in the slightly different sense “trespassing, unlawful entry”. For “house-search”, the older form is Middle High German hūssuoche, from Old High German hūssuohha. Compare Dutch huiszoeking.

noun:Hagedorn.tx: From Middle High German hagedorn, from Old High German hagudorn, from Proto-West Germanic *haguþorn.

noun:Hexagon.tx: From Latin hexagōnum, from Ancient Greek ἑξάγωνον (hexágōnon), substantivized neuter form of ἑξάγωνος (hexágōnos, “hexagonal”).

noun:Herold.tx: 14th century, from Middle High German heralt, from Old French héraut and its latinisation Medieval Latin heraldus, from Proto-West Germanic *heriwald. See herald for more.

noun:Hehl.tx: From Middle High German hæle (“concealment”), from Old High German hāla (“concealment”). Back-formation from hehlen.

noun:Halde.tx: From Middle High German halde, from Old High German halda, from hald, from a formation related to Proto-Germanic *halþaz (“sloping, inclined”) (from the slanted nature of large heaps). Other theories derive the word from Proto-West Germanic *hulli (“hill”).

noun:Hook.tx: From Middle Low German hôk (“corner, angle”), from Old Saxon hōk, from Proto-West Germanic *hōk, from Proto-Germanic *hōkaz. Compare the sense “small cluster of houses” in cognate Dutch hoek.

verb:herausziehen.tx: From Middle High German herūzziehen. Equivalent to heraus- + ziehen.

adj:höhnisch.tx: From Middle High German hœnisch. By surface analysis, Hohn + -isch.

noun:Holler.tx: Via Bavarian Holler from Middle High German holler, holer, holder, from Old High German holder, clipping of holuntar, from Proto-West Germanic *holantr.

adj:hanebüchen.tx: From earlier hagebüchen, from Middle High German hagenbüechīn, made from gnarly Hagebuche (“hornbeam”) wood.

noun:Heinze.tx: A High Germanization of the dialect form Hianz, Heanz, of uncertain origin. This may represent a form of the diminutive Heinz or it may be derived from hianz, a local variant of Bavarian hiaz (“hier”). (Compare Lemko, an ethnonym derived from a dialect term for "only".)

noun:Hinkel.tx: From Middle High German hünkel, from older huoniclīn, from Old High German huoninklīn, diminutive of huon, whence modern Huhn (“chicken”). The unrounded vowel -i- follows Rhine Franconian dialects, in which the word is chiefly used. Cognate with Luxembourgish Hénkel.

adj:hibbelig.tx: From hibbeln + -ig. The verb is a Rhine Franconian or East Central German form of hüpfeln, frequentative of hüpfen (“to hop”).

adj:hitzefrei.tx: Hitze (“heat”) + frei (“free, having the day off”).

adj:hämisch.tx: Inherited from Middle High German hemisch (originally “two-faced, false”), derived from Middle High German ham (“cover”), ultimately from Proto-West Germanic *hamō. Related to Hemd.

adj:hörig.tx: From Middle High German hœrec (“obedient”), equivalent to hören (“to hear, listen, obey”) + -ig. The historic sense after Middle Low German hōrich (“serfish”), derived from the same verb, but probably not (or not primarily) in the sense of “to obey”, but rather “to belong” (for which High German gehören and hence also gehörig in older German).

noun:Helfershelfer.tx: From late Middle High German helffershelffer.

noun:Helling.tx: Borrowed from Low German Hellinge, from Middle Low German hellinge, heldinge, from the verb helden (“to tilt, to hield”), Proto-Germanic *halþijaną.

noun:Hinde.tx: From Middle High German hinde, hinte, from Old High German hinta, hinna, from Proto-West Germanic *hindi.

noun:Handgriff.tx: Modern meanings since the 16th century. From Middle High German *hantgrif (only attested as hantgrift f (“the laying on of hands”)), from (Old High German hantgrif m (“handful, handgrip”), from Proto-West Germanic *handugripi (“handgrip”). Equivalent to Hand + Griff.

verb:hofieren.tx: Middle High German hovieren, from Hof + -ieren.

verb:hänseln.tx: 17th century, from Hanse (“guild”), from the hazing rituals performed on new members of guilds. Secondarily associated with the name Hans, which is sometimes used pejoratively (compare Hanswurst).

verb:herausgehen.tx: From Middle High German herūzgān. Equivalent to heraus- + gehen.

verb:herauskommen.tx: From Middle High German herūzkomen. Equivalent to heraus- + kommen.

verb:hinkommen.tx: From Middle High German hinkomen, from Old High German hinakweman, hinaqeman. Equivalent to hin- + kommen.

verb:heimsuchen.tx: From Middle High German heimsuochen. Equivalent to heim- + suchen.

noun:Herrenrasse.tx: From Herr (“gentleman, lord, master”) + -en- + Rasse (“race”), from the 19th century.

verb:hobeln.tx: Perhaps from Hobel + -en, which see. The noun has also been explained as a backformation from the verb, however.

verb:hinfahren.tx: From Middle High German hinvarn, from Old High German hinafaran. Equivalent to hin- + fahren.

noun:Halunke.tx: In literary use since ca. 1700. From Silesian East Central German Holomken (“servant”, 15th c.), from Old Czech holomek. Compare modern Czech holomek (“scoundrel”). The also attested sense “heathland warden, messenger” suggests merger with older Upper Sorbian *holank (attested as a name), diminutive of holan (“heathland dweller”), derived from hola (“heath”).

adj:heilsam.tx: From Middle High German heilsam, from Old High German heilsam, heilisam, from Proto-West Germanic *hailasam, *hailisam, from Proto-Germanic *hailasamaz, *hailisamaz, equivalent to heil + -sam. Cognate with English wholesome.

noun:Hallodri.tx: From Southern German, Austrian Hallodri, probably from Allotria (“tomfoolery”).

noun:Herrengedeck.tx: From Herr (“gentleman”) + -en- + Gedeck (“place setting”), implying that it is the standard order for men.

noun:Hungerhaken.tx: Hunger + Haken, perhaps influenced by Hungerharke.

verb:hochschlafen.tx: From hoch (“high, up, upwards”) + schlafen (“to sleep”), as an alteration of hocharbeiten (“to work one’s way up”).

phrase:Hopfen und Malz ist verloren.tx: Literally, “hop and malt are lost”. Perhaps an antithesis to the phrase Hopfen und Malz, Gott erhalt's, which see.

phrase:Holland ist offen.tx: Literally, “Holland is open”. From Central Franconian do es offe Holland, explained in the Rheinisches Wörterbuch as a pun on holle (“to take, fetch”), cognate of German holen.

noun:Hin.tx: Borrowed from Hebrew הִין, from Egyptian hnw (“jar, unit of liquid volume”): h:n-nw-w-W22.

noun:Holster.tx: From Low German Holster, from Middle Low German holster, from Old Saxon *holster, from Proto-Germanic *hulistrą. The word was borrowed directly from Low German (early 19th c. or earlier), but remained rare until the later 20th c., when it was reinforced by English holster, itself of Low German origin.

noun:Halbwelt.tx: Calque of French demi-monde, halb + Welt.

noun:Herzblut.tx: From Middle High German herzebluot. Equivalent to Herz (“heart”) + Blut (“blood”).

verb:hingeben.tx: From Middle High German hingëben, from Old High German hinagëban. Equivalent to hin- + geben.

noun:Heimstatt.tx: Heim + Statt. Cognate to English homestead, Dutch heemstede and Swedish hemstad.

adj:habhaft.tx: Inherited from Middle High German habhaft, equivalent to haben + -haft.

adj:hautnah.tx: Haut + nah, literally “near to the skin”. Compare Japanese 身近 (mijika, literally “near to the body”).

noun:Herzeleid.tx: Herze- (“heart”) (obsolete combining form of Herz) + Leid

noun:Himmelfahrtskommando.tx: Determinative compound of Himmelfahrt (“ascension”) + -s- + Kommando, literally “command of ascension to heaven”.

adj:hirnverbrannt.tx: Hirn (“brain”) + verbrannt (“burnt”), a calque of French cerveau brûlé.

noun:Heidenlärm.tx: Heide (“heathen”) + -n- (“noise”) + Lärm; as in Heidenangst, Heidengeld, Heidenspaß, and other compounds, Heiden- serves to emphasise the second part.

noun:Homoehe.tx: Homo + Ehe, equivalent to homo- + Ehe.

verb:höhnen.tx: From Middle High German hœnen, from Old High German *hōnen, from Proto-West Germanic *haunijan, from Proto-Germanic *haunijaną.

verb:hinwerfen.tx: From Middle High German hinwerfen, from Old High German hinawerfan. Equivalent to hin- + werfen.

intj:hosianna.tx: Ultimately from Biblical Hebrew הוֹשַׁע נָא (hōsha‘ nā, “please save”).

noun:Hippe.tx: From Middle High German heppe, happe, hipe, from Old High German heppa, hīpe, happa, from Proto-West Germanic *happjā. Compare Dutch heep.

noun:Hutzel.tx: From Middle High German hutzel, hützel.

noun:Hundsfott.tx: Hund + -s- and a fossilized dialectal form of Fotze; a standard insult with fixed fine in the middle range during the Early Modern Age.

noun:Hörensagen.tx: From Middle High German hœrsagen (14th c.). Equivalent to hören (“to hear”) + sagen (“to say”). Compare English hearsay, which is of similar age.

noun:Handhabe.tx: From Middle High German hanthabe, from Old High German hanthaba, hanthabī.

noun:Homeoffice.tx: Borrowed from English home office. The sense "working from home" is a pseudo-anglicism.

verb:heimführen.tx: From Middle High German heimvüeren, from Old High German heimfuoren. Equivalent to heim- + führen.

noun:Hausnummer.tx: A determinative compound of Haus (“house”) + Nummer (“number”).

noun:Heros.tx: 18th century, from Latin hērōs, from Ancient Greek ἥρως (hḗrōs).

intj:hoppla.tx: Onomatopoeic; compare English hoopla, French houp-là, hop-là and Italian oplà.

noun:Hospiz.tx: Late 18th century, shortened from earlier Hospitium (17th c.), from Latin hospitium.

noun:Hypochondrie.tx: 18th century back-formation from hypochondrisch, presumably influenced by French hypochondrie, from New Latin hypochondria.

noun:Hassrede.tx: Hass + Rede. The uncountable use is a semantic loan from English hate speech, though there exists an intermediate usage based on the indefinite plural.

verb:halluzinieren.tx: Borrowed from French halluciner + -ieren, from Latin ālūcinor.

noun:Heuerling.tx: From Middle Low German *hürling, from Old Saxon *hūriling, from Proto-West Germanic *hūʀijuling. Compare English hireling, Dutch huurling.

noun:Heinzelmännchen.tx: From Heinzel + Männchen, diminutive of Heinz.

noun:Hammelsprung.tx: From Hammel (“wether”) + Sprung (“jump”). Thought to be from the idea that (most of) the delegates follow their faction leaders like sheep follow bellwethers.

verb:hudeln.tx: From Hudel. Compare Dutch hoetelen, English huddle.

pt: to hop, to skip, to bounce; to jump
noun:Hüpfer.tx: hüpfen (“to hop, to skip, to bounce; to jump”) + -er

noun:Hagestolz.tx: Inherited from Middle High German hagestolz, modified by the adjective underlying stolz from hagestolt, hagestalt, from Old High German hagastalt, hagustalt, from Proto-West Germanic *hagustald, Proto-Germanic *hagustaldaz.

verb:hotzen.tx: Of unclear origin, perhaps from a variant of Middle High German hutzen (“to move back and forth”), either of imitative origin or otherwise possibly from Proto-West Germanic *hottōn (“to shake, toss”), from Proto-Germanic *hud- (“to swing, rock, shake”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)ket- or *kwēt- (“to shake, rock back and forth”). See also English hod (“to bob up and down”) and French hocher (“to shake”).

noun:Homöostase.tx: Coined from Ancient Greek ὅμοιος (hómoios), and from Ancient Greek στάσις (stásis).

noun:Hämorrhoide.tx: From Latin haemorrhoidae, from Ancient Greek αἱμορροίδες (haimorrhoídes), from αἱμόρροος (haimórrhoos, “flowing with blood”), from αἷμα (haîma, “blood”) and the root of ῥέω (rhéō, “flow”).

noun:Hähnchenkeule.tx: From Hähnchen (“chicken”) + Keule (“club; leg of an animal”).

noun:Hendl.tx: Via Bavarian Hendl from Middle High German hendl, hendel, henel, from Old High German *henil, diminutive of Old High German hano (“cock, rooster”), equivalent to Hahn + -el.

verb:hinziehen.tx: From Middle High German hinziehen, from Old High German hinaziohan. Equivalent to hin- + ziehen

noun:Harmonika.tx: Borrowed from English harmonica. First attested in the 18th century.

noun:Hinfahrt.tx: From Middle High German hinvart, from Old High German hinafart. Equivalent to hin- + Fahrt.

intj:hoppala.tx: Onomatopoeic; compare English hoopla and French houp-là.

noun:Hoppla.tx: Onomatopoeic; compare English hoopla and French houp-là; nominalisation of hoppla/hoppala.

adv:halbmast.tx: Calque of English half-mast, from halb + Mast.

noun:Hühnerei.tx: From Huhn (“chicken, hen”) + Ei (“egg”) with epenthesis of -er including umlaut.

phrase:hätte, hätte, Fahrradkette.tx: Literally, “would have, would have, bicycle chain”, mockingly echoing the subjunctive hätte, with Fahrradkette as a nonsensical term added purely for the rhyme while matching the meter. Likely coined in the TV comedy Stromberg in 2007, further popularized in 2013 when Chancellor-candidate Peer Steinbrück used it in an interview.

verb:hochschätzen.tx: Univerbation of hoch (“highly”) + schätzen (“to consider, appreciate”).

noun:Honigmond.tx: From Honig + Mond, a calque of French lune de miel, itself after English honeymoon.

noun:Heißsporn.tx: Ca. 1800, from heiß (“hot”) + Sporn (“spur”), a calque of English hotspur.

noun:Helles.tx: Nominalized neuter of hell (“bright”), after its clear colour.

verb:herumfuchteln.tx: herum- + fuchteln, literally “to wave around aimlessly”

verb:haushalten.tx: From Middle High German hūshalten, equivalent to Haus (“house”) + halten (“to hold”). Possibly derived from Haushalt, though this noun is attested slightly later.

noun:Hautevolee.tx: From French (gens de) haute volée (“first-class people”).

phrase:Hopfen und Malz, Gott erhalt's.tx: Literally, “hop and malt, may God preserve it”.

noun:Happening.tx: Unadapted borrowing from English happening, from Middle English *happenynge, *happnynge.

verb:harpunieren.tx: Borrowed from Dutch harpoeneren, from Dutch harpoen, possibly from French harpon.

noun:Halligalli.tx: Perhaps from English hully gully, a popular dance in the 1960s.

noun:Hypnotikum.tx: From Late Latin hypnoticus, from Ancient Greek ὑπνωτικός (hupnōtikós, “inclined to sleep, putting to sleep, sleepy”), from ὑπνῶ (hupnô, “I put to sleep”), from ὕπνος (húpnos, “sleep”).

noun:Hundewetter.tx: From Hund + -e- + Wetter. Compare Dutch hondenweer, French temps de chien, Italian tempo da cani.

intj:heidewitzka.tx: Popularized by the 1936 Kölsch song Heidewitzka, Herr Kapitän by Karl Berbuer (also known as the Müllemer Böötche). Ultimately in all likelihood onomatopoeic. It seems unclear whether the word was coined by Berbuer or already existed before. Many commentators think that the phrase Heidewitzka, Herr Kapitän (roughly “Huzzah, Mr. Captain”) was a covert parody of Heil Hitler.

noun:Handbreite.tx: From Middle High German hantbreite, from Old High German hantbreita, equivalent to Hand + Breite. Cognate to English handbreadth, Saterland Frisian Houndebratte (“handbreadth”), West Frisian hânbreedte (“handbreadth”), Dutch handbreedte (“handbreadth”), Swedish handsbredd (“handbreadth”), Norwegian håndsbredd (“handbreadth”), Icelandic handbreidd (“handbreadth”).

noun:Hausgenosse.tx: From Middle High German hūsgenōze, hūsgenōz, from Old High German hūsginōzo, hūsginōz. Equivalent to Haus + Genosse.

verb:herumspuken.tx: From herum + spuken. Cognate with Dutch rondspoken.

noun:Hintertreffen.tx: hinter- (“behind, back”) + Treffen (“battle”) (18th century). Referred originally to the rear part of an army not taking part in a battle that would not partake in the benefits of victory.

noun:Heliport.tx: From English heliport. By surface analysis, Heli + Port.

adj:heroinsüchtig.tx: From Heroin + süchtig, equivalent to Heroinsucht + -ig.

noun:Handlungsreisender.tx: From Handlung (“trade, shop”) + -s- + Reisender (“traveling person, traveler”).

noun:Hetzkampagne.tx: From hetzen (“to chase; to agitate”) + Kampagne (“campaign”).

noun:Hikikomori.tx: Borrowed from Japanese 引きこもり (hikikomori).

adv:halbtags.tx: From Halbtag (“half a day”) + -s (adverbial suffix). Alternative surface analysis, halb (“half”) + tags (“days, during the day”).

noun:Hochbegabter.tx: Nominalisation of the adjective hochbegabt (“highly talented, gifted”). By surface analysis, hoch + Begabter.

noun:Hartriegel.tx: From Middle High German hartrügele, from Old High German hart(t)rugil. The meaning of the second element is unclear.

noun:Handstreich.tx: Hand + Streich. Originally a synonym for Handschlag (“handshake”). In the early 19th century repurposed as a calque of French coup de main.

noun:Hutschnur.tx: Compound of Hut + Schnur. Attested as similar Old High German huotilsnuor, huotilīnessnur.

noun:Hochschulreife.tx: 19th century, Hochschule + Reife, if at some point meant formally then translating the foreignist Maturität in compounds.

phrase:Hals Maul.tx: Literally, “neck, mouth”. A humorous reanalysis of halt's Maul.

noun:Heimreise.tx: Deverbal from heimreisen or Heim + Reise.

verb:herausbrechen.tx: From Middle High German herūzbrechen. Equivalent to heraus- + brechen.

noun:Huckel.tx: Probably a variation of Hügel, originally East Central German.

noun:Holdrio.tx: Substantivization of the joyful interjection holdrio.

noun:Heimlich-Manöver.tx: Partial calque of English Heimlich maneuver.

noun:Hitlerfaschismus.tx: From Hitler + Faschismus. In Socialist parlance used to avoid any mention of the term Nationalsozialismus or its abbreviations.

verb:heimsen.tx: Possibly from rare Middle High German heimsen, from Old High German *heimezzen, *heimezen, from Proto-West Germanic *haimattjan. Otherwise from Heim + -en with intrusive -s-.

noun:Hedgefonds.tx: Borrowed from English hedge fund. Surface analysis yields Hedge (“hedge”) + Fonds (“fund”).

noun:Historiografie.tx: From earler Historiographie, learned borrowing from New Latin historiographia.

noun:Hiersein.tx: Univerbation of hier + sein, literally “being here”.

noun:Höllenstein.tx: From Hölle (“hell”) + -n- + Stein (“stone”), calque of Latin lapis īnfernālis.

adv:halbe-halbe.tx: Literally, “half-half”, from halb. The -e potentially represents an adjective ending corresponding to an elided noun. The phrase seemingly first occured in "halbe-halbe machen", which Küpper dates to 1910, later generalizing into use with other verbs.

noun:Hochfinanz.tx: From hoch + Finanz, a calque of French haute finance.

noun:Herzenssache.tx: From Herz + -ens- + Sache. Compare Hungarian szívügy.

noun:Headset.tx: Borrowed from English headset, from head + set.

noun:Hometrainer.tx: Pseudo-anglicism, derived from home + trainer. Compare Dutch hometrainer.
